When merging two or more images taken at different times with a telescope, the point spread function (PSF) of the resulting image is not simply the average of the individual PSFs due to the varying brightness of the stars used for calibration. In fact, the effect goes beyond a basic average, influenced by factors including the ratio of bright to dark pixels in the PSFs, and must take into account sub-pixel image shifting, which can lead to misinterpretation. We present a reliable mathematical expression for the PSF of combined images, and provide supporting code for use in practice. The code is specifically tailored for use with the PyRAF language, and includes examples illustrating its effectiveness. In particular, we demonstrate that the ratio of bright to dark pixels in the PSFs can be utilized to improve the accuracy of photometric calibration, and that the PSF ratio can be utilized to detect and identify changes in the telescope's field of view. The proposed method has been successfully tested in various applications, including the long-term monitoring of selected Galactic and Gravitational Wave Legacy Project stars. In general, the method is expected to be of significant benefit in a wide range of astronomical research, and will become an essential tool for data analysis in the upcoming Vera C. Rubin Observatory, where it will play a pivotal role in meeting science requirements. The proposed method is versatile, and can be easily adapted for use in a wide range of astronomical research, incorporating various reduction and co-addition techniques. The results presented are primarily based on data from the Legacy Survey of Dark Energy (LSDFE), also known as the DESI Legacy Survey. The code is specifically tailored to meet the data analysis needs of the Galaxies and Cosmology science team in the DESI project. The proposed method is expected to be of significant benefit in a wide range of astronomical research, and will become an essential tool for data analysis in future astronomical research, including the study of the development of galaxies over cosmic time and the observation of Gravitational Wave signals. The associated Python code is publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/ramiromaravito/psf_ratio.git. Furthermore, the study also explores the domain-percolation probability in the context of these graphs under the infinite-cluster criterion and shows that this model shares similarities with a recent generalization of the Ising model's phase transition behavior. This investigation concerns the Navier-Stimes equations in three-dimensional space with periodic conditions. We demonstrate that for initial data with sub-critical Fourier norms, the solution set forms a single continuous function over time. In contrast, for data with critical Fourier norms, we show the non-existence of globally defined solutions beyond a limited time frame. Our analysis draws upon similar reasoning employed by Bourgain and Li in studying the nonlinear Schrodinger equations. This study also builds upon earlier work by Esposito, Kowalczyk, and Wolanski, which examined the Navier-Stimes equations in terms of the maximum norm. Unlike those studies, this research focuses on the most extreme measure - the L∞-norm, utilizing novel techniques and providing fresh insights into the behavior of solutions near equilibrium. Furthermore, we identify a critical time threshold for solutions initiated by data slightly exceeding the critical threshold, marking a key deviation from maximum-norm-based results that predict the solutions would approach equilibrium within that same critical time frame, regardless of the measure used. Interestingly, this study also reveals that multiple solutions can develop at roughly half the critical time frame, a phenomenon that has no analogue in maximum-norm-based results and is unlikely to be replicated in other settings. Lastly, we believe that this study's results can be extended to encompass additional equations, a hypothesis that is supported by generalised theorems included in this investigation. These theorems allow for the smooth transition from any sub-critical measure to another sub-critical measure. In particular, we demonstrate that this solution will remain defined for at least a limited time frame in terms of Lebesgue measure, a prediction that is grounded in the theory surrounding many dissipative PDEs. In effect, we have successfully generalised a widely-held conjecture surrounding the nonlinear Schrodinger equations, a notable achievement that is accompanied by the prediction of multiple solutions at roughly half the critical time frame, a prediction that is novel and unlikely to be replicated in other settings. Additionally, we believe that this study's results can be extended to encompass a range of other dissipative equations, a hypothesis that is grounded in the theory surrounding many dissipative PDEs. A key obstacle to the widespread acceptance of quantum computing lies in the truth that, at present, there are no established methods for confirming that quantum algorithms are indeed delivering the correct results. Although various techniques exist for verifying the accuracy of quantum calculations in relation to their execution time, and another set of methods enables us to verify their accuracy in relation to their reliability, all such methods compromise on at least one of these fronts. However, a new study presents a traditional validation method that requires neither excessive computation time nor uncertainty in outcomes, employing instead classical techniques that were developed long ago. At the heart of this new approach lies a straightforward yet innovative connection between unitary operators, established by matrix representation, which in turn enables us to extend a known theorem concerning classical measurement outcomes to the realm of quantum computing. Furthermore, this study examines several prevalent algorithms for linear problems, including solving systems of linear equations and linear regression, and demonstrates that their quantum versions do not offer any significant advantages over their classical counterparts. These results shed new light on the efficacy of quantum computing and highlight potential avenues for further exploration. Moreover, this study introduces a novel paradigm for classifying verification methods and establishes a connection between this classification and a fundamental concept in quantum computing known as measurement noise. Ultimately, this study presents an innovative approach to addressing a critical challenge facing quantum computing, and its findings are expected to contribute significantly to further research in this field. A comprehensive draft of this study is available on arXiv, titled "No Speedup: The Generation of Bounded Nature in Unitary Operators Employing Fast Algorithms". Key Observations:

 1. There are three primary approaches to verifying the accuracy of quantum algorithms, each compromising on a different front: time, duration, or certainty. This study presents an innovative method that requires neither excessive computation time nor uncertainty in outcomes.

 2. A fundamental obstacle in verifying the accuracy of quantum algorithms lies in the truth that, at present, there are no established methods for confirming that these algorithms are indeed delivering the correct results.

Although various techniques exist for verifying the accuracy of quantum calculations in relation to their execution time (fast algorithms), and another set of methods enables us to verify their accuracy in relation to their reliability (noisy algorithms), all such methods compromise on at least one of these fronts.

 4. A key challenge facing quantum computing is addressing the critical challenge of verifying the accuracy of these algorithms in a timely and reliable manner.

Recent breakthroughs in implicit neural representations have enabled the creation of training-friendly functions for complex 3D objects. This innovation has significant potential for the modeling of biological cell types, which are intricately shaped and varied. Current approaches to cell modeling, however, rely on either semi-implicit methods like level sets or solely render cell types without enabling generative modeling. This research explores the application of implicit neural representations in cell modeling, leveraging the versatility of neural networks. By combining neural representations with a range of observing points, we demonstrate the efficacy of training generative models of biological cells through the latent space of neural networks. The results showcase implicit neural representations as a valuable tool in modeling cellular shapes, offering the capability for generative modeling. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexkoch/cell-implicit-neural-representations. The cell models are hosted on the CellAtlas platform at https://cellatlas.org/cells/#/search.

Two commonly used visualizations for spatial information in biological systems are spatial projections and spatial depictions by similarity. Unlike static methods, dynamic approaches such as reinforcement learning can optimize spatial representations by efficiently utilizing high-dimensional data like neural networks. By applying this to the depictions of space, we suggest a dynamic and adaptive method that learns high-dimensional depictions of space in an efficient manner, similar to how reinforcement learning optimizes complex decisions. This leads to a dynamic and adaptive visualization of space that learns structure automatically, including notable features, scaling well for dimensions, and producing consistent results across different random initializations. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in identifying clusters, detecting complex data distributions, and revealing organization in datasets with no predefined labels. Finally, we apply this approach to the depictions of neural populations in the mammalian brain, revealing organized structures in the retinal map and the somatosensory cortex map. We believe this method will be useful for neural codings and spatial representations in biological systems. The remote sound source localization (SSL) task involves identifying the three-dimensional coordinates of a sound origin with minimal audio signal information, a challenging problem in remote sensing. Due to its practical applications and complexity, researchers prefer to tackle the related sound classification and localization task, which requires mapping audio spectra to three-dimensional coordinates. A related problem is sound position detection, where we aim to find the three-dimensional coordinates of sound sources within a predefined area. In this research, we propose a new dataset that includes spatially-mixed audio recordings from multiple sound sources in a home environment and use a full convolutional neural network to simultaneously locate sound sources and classify them. By applying channel rotation and using rectangular filters, our network can effectively process spatially-mixed recordings and distinguish the underlying sound sources. By training and testing our network on the new dataset, we demonstrate its ability to accurately detect sound sources and identify them in various spatial configurations. Notably, our network achieved high accuracy in a difficult scenario where sound sources were closely grouped and reached performance parity with a more complex network that used more sophisticated rectangular filters. The proposed dataset and related approaches are expected to be useful in a range of remote sensing applications, including robotics and human-robot interaction. Concurrent transmission based wireless communication systems have the ability to send multiple data signals at the same time, over the same frequency channel, in contrast to traditional systems that can only transmit one signal at a time. This approach has drawn the attention of researchers due to its potential to significantly boost throughput, using techniques such as superposition coding (ENC). In this paper, we take a closer look at various applications of ENC in wireless systems, specifically in scenarios involving multiple users, interference, and packet transmission. Key applications examined include multi-user superposition coding, where encoding is done for multiple users at the same time, but with users being able to distinguish their individual messages; and scenarios with multiple sources of interference, where techniques such as precoding and encoding for multiple users are explored in order to mitigate interference and maximize system performance, using metrics such as sum rate capacity as a benchmark. Furthermore, we explore more recent developments in wireless communication systems, specifically those involving applications where data is transmitted in the form of packets, such as in wireless local area networks (WLANs), where encoding is done for multiple users at the same time and various techniques such as joint encoding and transmission precoding are used to enhance system performance, using metrics such as sum rate capacity as a benchmark. Ultimately, we look at future research directions in this area and how further study could lead to enhanced performance in wireless communication systems using techniques such as machine learning. In the end, we see that superposition encoding has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of wireless communication systems. Key words: Wireless Communication, Superposition Coding, Precoding, Multi-User Systems, Interference, Convex Optimization, Successive Convex Approximation, Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, Alternating Minimization.

To achieve this, we modeled the dynamics of quantum states represented by a small number of quantum fields, relying on Markovian assumptions. The resulting quantum Fokker-Planck equation mirrors the behavior of its classical counterpart but also incorporates key quantum features. In the context of feedback regulation, this approach enables us to examine the interplay between quantum effects and biological complexity. Our analysis focuses on a specific case study - the regulation of NF-κB signaling pathways - and explores the potential for quantum effects to persist at the level of individual proteins, given the high temperature and short lifetime of these proteins. These findings support the notion that quantum effects can significantly influence the regulation of biological systems, even in environments with harsh conditions. Furthermore, we identified the distinct signatures of quantum effects that can be detected through experimentation. To verify our theoretical model, we suggested feasible experiments that could be conducted using cutting-edge technology. These proposed experiments aim to reconcile the current understanding of the double well experiment with the predictions made by quantum thermodynamics. In the process, we highlighted the unique advantages of approaching thermodynamics from a quantum perspective. This research explores two-dimensional blocked discs, one of which occupies the center, surrounded by an array of identical cylindrical obstacles arranged in a linear sequence, all moving through a narrow, winding channel. Initially, our analysis focuses on scenarios where the obstruction sequence alternates between two and three elements. Using regular pencil states at the entrance, we derive, through analytical methods, the specific arrangements of polarized states that correspond to unique egress masses for both the $(2n)$ and $(2n+1)$ cases. Notably, for any given egress mass, there exists exactly one corresponding regular pencil state. Furthermore, for any given number of discs $N$, there are exactly $2N+1$ possible egress masses. Research into El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has concentrated on analyzing the unique characteristics of two distinct ENSO varieties, which have implications for understanding how precipitation patterns change globally. Rare ENSO events (REEs) are characterized by a significant departure from usual variations in the phenomenon. We investigated how REEs are different from other ENSO events in terms of their impact on global precipitation patterns, using various statistical measures, including multivariate linear regression analysis, principal component analysis, and random forests. Our results show that REEs have distinct spatial and temporal effects on global precipitation, affecting areas that don't usually experience extreme precipitation, including parts of Asia, Europe, and Africa during non-hat seasons. In contrast, other ENSO events have little effect on these regions. Additionally, REEs have enhanced impacts on various precipitation-related indices, such as extreme precipitation in Australia and coastal South Africa. We also found that REEs have distinct temporal effects on global precipitation, including a notable split in their impacts on regions that experience seasonal and non-seasonal precipitation variations. Notably, REEs have amplified effects on areas that don't usually experience seasonal precipitation variations, including parts of Asia, Europe, and Africa. Our study provides a statistical understanding of the distinct variations in the impacts of two different ENSO types on global precipitation patterns, which can be used to improve the representation of rare ENSO events in global climate models. Improving our ability to simulate REEs in climate models has various practical applications, including reducing uncertainty in global precipitation forecasts, refining regional climate risk assessments, and enhancing early warning systems for extreme precipitation events. Furthermore, our study's approach to analyzing rare climate events can be applied to various other climate phenomena, such as La Ni\~na events. This material exhibits a flat band at the Fermi level and shows indications of flat band physics influencing its electronic behavior. However, this behavior is adversely impacted by magnetic field, resulting in decreased resistivity at low temperatures regardless of field orientation. This adverse magnetoresistance cannot be fully attributed to intrinsic flat band effects and is influenced by existing magnetic domains in the material. Increasing Ta content enhances the adverse magnetoresistance and flat band influence, suggesting that these effects are interrelated. Our findings reveal the potential for flat band physics to significantly affect electronic properties and suggest further research using advanced experimental and theoretical techniques to fully understand these phenomena. This includes using neutron scattering and first-principles calculations to confirm our hypotheses. On the other hand, incorporating a small amount of Ir, which interacts strongly with electrons, results in gapped electronic bands and eliminates both flat band and adverse magnetoresistance features. This indicates that the negative magnetoresistance can be attributed to multi-orbital correlations facilitated by a flat band. This unique behavior is a result of multiple electronic bands interacting with each other in a specific type of lattice structure, known as the kagome lattice. This discovery represents one of the few known instances where flat bands have been shown to influence the negative magnetoresistance observed in many multi-orbital systems. Moreover, we propose that our material observations are in line with a flat band induced Fermi Arctic phenomenon, which occurs in systems with high point density and is characterized by a gap in the density of states at the Fermi level. This phenomenon is not fully explained by existing magnetic order but is instead driven by the flat band physics. This discovery represents a significant breakthrough in understanding the relationship between flat band physics and electronic properties. This study presents an innovative approach to determining the state of synchronization between two time series, enabling comparison with established methods. We utilize cross-correlation analysis and cross-recurrence plots to develop a predictive model for synchronization states, which is then applied to the S&P 500 and NASDAQ indices. Notably, our results reveal that this method accurately forecasts non-synchronized and synchronized states in both indices up to 2 days in advance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in an optimization problem by incorporating it into a decision tree, which successfully predicts synchronization states in the S&P 500 index with high accuracy. We also highlight the merit of our non-invasive technique, noting that it outperforms other methods such as generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (GARCH) models, which often fail to accurately forecast synchronization in volatile markets like the US shares market. GARCH models have previously been assumed to be robust due to their widespread use, but our research indicates that they can be less effective in certain environments. Consequently, we suggest integrating the proposed cross-recurrence plotting method into a GARCH model to enhance its predictive accuracy for synchronization states. Ultimately, this research contributes to the body of knowledge on financial time series analysis and points out potential avenues for further exploration. Additionally, we publicly share the code used in this study to facilitate replication, which comprises elements from various open-source libraries including MatLab, Python, and Stan. Enhancing CTR forecasting for new promotions requires accurate prediction of user response to unseen visual materials. This research addresses this challenge by converting CTR forecasting into a multi-view image enhancement task, incorporating explicit enhancement objectives to refine predicted clicks. The model architecture comprises a modular structure, incorporating the encoder, cross-modal encoder, decoder, and CTR predictor modules. The cross-modal encoder integrates the vision module with the classifier module, enabling the combination of visual features with click predictions. The model is trained end-to-end, leveraging a dataset enhanced with automatic scaling of visual materials. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance on public benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results in CTR forecasting for e-commerce platforms. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Chen-550/CENet.1.0.0.

The rise of location-based services has sparked interest in understanding the impact of location privacy on user anonymity. A method called location privacy under conditional expectations (LPCE) guarantees users' geographic privacy by revealing aggregated location data after meeting a predetermined privacy threshold based on the Kalman filter's predictive and retrospective distances. This study assesses the effectiveness of LPCE in maintaining user anonymity through analysis of entropy metrics. The investigation involves simulating LPCE using actual GPS data from various individuals with distinct walking speeds. The results demonstrate that LPCE can maintain the anonymity of low-speed walkers even with a privacy threshold of 30 meters, while high-speed walkers require a higher privacy threshold. Furthermore, LPCE's performance is evaluated against two alternative location privacy methods, revealing its efficiency and simplicity in protecting users' geographic privacy. The integration of LPCE into location-based services has the potential to significantly enhance users' anonymity. A novel location privacy framework, which incorporates a location privacy module and a distance-based learning module, is introduced to maintain users' geographic privacy in location-based services. The architecture's efficacy is validated through a location privacy prototyping process involving a community-based smart parking application as a practical example. The prototyping involves collecting real GPS data from a group of participants using a low-cost device, who are divided into high-speed and low-speed walkers based on their average walking speeds. The results of entropy analysis for this group are presented as a heatmap, illustrating the connection between LPCE's privacy threshold and entropy levels. Two location privacy methods, including a location privacy service and geofencing, are analyzed and compared with LPCE in maintaining users' geographic privacy. The analysis shows that LPCE requires minimal user input and can be efficiently used by a location privacy service to protect users' privacy. Additionally, LPCE's distance-based learning approach can be utilized to develop personalized location privacy configurations, including setting a preferred privacy threshold according to each user's walking speed. The connection between LPCE's distance metrics and its privacy threshold can be leveraged to create a location privacy dashboard, which enables users to monitor their location privacy, including the distance and angle of their past and predictive locations. The location privacy dashboard is presented as a heat map for high-speed and low-speed walkers, illustrating LPCE's effectiveness and simplicity in maintaining users' geographic privacy. Using a tight-binding model with 6s and 6p orbitals for H$_3$S, we investigate how its electronic structure changes with pressure in relation to hole filling. Considering the density of states at the Fermi level as a function of pressure, we observe a significant increase at the Fermi level with pressure, consistent with experimental data. However, our results overestimate the increase and the critical temperature based on the linearized Eliashberg equations. Moreover, we find that the critical temperature's dependence on nuclear mass enhances with pressure, but not in proportion as predicted by calculations using the linearized Eliashberg equations. These observations suggest that the superconductivity in H$_3$S is not fully explained by the variable-band model and the van Hove enhancement plays a crucial role in the unusual pressure-dependent behavior of this system. Therefore, to accurately understand the high-temperature superconductivity in H$_3$S, the effects of van Hove enhancement and nuclear influence must be taken into account. Based on our calculations, we predict that the critical temperature will reach 288 K at a pressure of 147 GPa. Our observations are consistent with experimental findings and provide a framework for further investigations of this and related systems. Additionally, our results can be generalized to other hydrides as they exhibit a similar band structure and the van Hove singularity is anticipated to play a crucial role in their superconductivity. The prediction of superconductivity up to 100 K in N$_2$ and 150 K in P$_2$ and 160 K in AsH$_3$ in our previous study using similar models further strengthens this notion. Therefore, these materials are potential candidates to achieve ultra-high-temperature superconductivity up to 100 K and the van Hove enhancement and variable-band structure due to dimensional crossover or electron-phonon interaction may play crucial roles in achieving this goal. Lastly, we propose an alternative strategy to achieve 100 K superconductivity by utilizing pressure-induced crossover from a high-density to a low-density Van Hove singularity while maintaining the strength of the electron-phonon interaction. This concept can be generalized to other systems and may provide a new paradigm for achieving ultra-high-temperature superconductivity. To achieve this, we first illustrate the underlying mathematical structure of mean effect within a general statistical model using tools from convex analysis. Next, we identify the key properties required for mean effect to function as a causal summary by drawing on the work of Suárez and colleagues. With these foundational aspects clarified, we establish a clear distinction between stimulating and effective causes, demonstrating that mean effect is ultimately a measure that ascribes causal significance to instrumental variables as well. This revised understanding of Fisher's mean effect theory is then compared to the principles of Bayesian statistics, particularly as interpreted by Reichenbach, to highlight their striking similarities. Finally, we reflect on the broader implications of this causal paradigm, noting its potential to inform the development of novel statistical methods and therapeutic strategies. Ultimately, this article seeks to convey the profound causal insights that can be gleaned from the work of Fisher. We hope that this mathematical reimagining of his ideas will inspire fresh insights and innovations. To that end, we propose the term "Fisherian innovation" to capture the causal significance of mean effect theory. In this spirit, we encourage readers to embark on their own imaginative journeys, envisioning the stimulating causes that can bring about health-promoting changes. As Fisher himself recognized, the causal structures that underpin his theory of mean effect remain largely unknown. To fill this knowledge gap, we believe that Fisherian innovation – a fusion of cutting-edge biology, informatics, and innovative thinking – holds the key to uncovering the underlying causal mechanisms that can reshape our understanding of medicine and inform therapeutic strategies. We envision a future research agenda that can harness the wisdom of Fisher's mean effect theory, translating it into a suite of novel therapeutic interventions, informative risk models, and predictive tools, all grounded in a clear vision of causal structure and function. A key factor in creating realistic humanoid robots is the ability to accurately replicate human gaits. While existing robots can walk using control methods that don't require actuator feedback, their efficiency and resilience are limited compared to actual human walking. This paper explores the potential benefits of active foot movement in improving robot gaits, testing the hypothesis that powered ankle movement can enhance stability and efficiency. To this end, a simplified model of the ANUBIS humanoid robot was created using a multi-body dynamics tool, simulating walking patterns with and without active foot movement. The results indicate that incorporating powered ankle movement can increase walking speeds and reduce energy consumption by up to 30%. Building on these findings, we propose a strategy for using propulsion-assisted bipedal movement to achieve similar improvements in existing robots. This approach involves timing the foot push-off to maximize the transfer of propulsive energy to the upper body. The resulting increase in potential energy can then be harnessed to improve walking efficiency and resilience. The proposed strategy was successfully validated using numerical simulations, showing promising results. Specifically, a 30% increase in walking speeds was demonstrated for the LittleDog robot, and similar improvements in efficiency are anticipated for other bipedal robots. The potential applications of this research include enhancing the performance of existing humanoid robots and developing new ones with improved walking capabilities. We developed a rigorous visual relocalization technique that uses 3D surfel maps as a guiding framework, combining geometric and photometric considerations. By creating a detailed map of visual features during an initial exploration phase, we enable precise location recalculations when only partial observations from memory are available at re localization time. Although earlier methods relied on approximate geometric matches, our innovative approach leverages a precise 2D association strategy facilitated by surfel map structure. Moreover, we introduce a novel learning-based method for generating descriptive features that resist common image transformations, resulting in a high performance relocalization outcome. Our technique has been successfully applied and showed results on challenging real-world datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we demonstrate the scalability of our method by successfully applying it to scenarios with expanded scales and complexity. Comprehensive technical details and source code are available online for reproduction of our methods and experiments. Experimental evaluation showed that our technique achieved 80% successful relocalizations within 2 meters of error, outperforming the best existing method by 30 percentage points. Additionally, we successfully relocalized 80% of times on a self-driving route that was recorded over a year ago with less than 0.5 meters error. These outcomes clearly indicate the efficacy of our approach.

Mobile devices are generating considerable amounts of data, particularly in the context of computer vision. This research proposes federated semi-supervised learning, a novel approach that enables on-device image classification tasks by leveraging a vast amount of untagged data and a limited set of labeled data specific to each device, without compromising security and data sovereignty. We identify a significant issue with training models in such a framework - the local models are inconsistent due to different ambient data and ambiguously classify certain classes, causing degradation in performance. To tackle this challenge, we've developed Ambiguity Reduction (AR) for FSSL, a framework that employs global ambient data to prune inconsistent local models and clarify class ambiguities. This results in more accurate and reliable models, outperforming existing solutions and performing significantly better on real-world datasets. For example, in the federated semi-supervised learning test, AR increases the accuracy of training models by up to 27% compared to current best approaches, while also enhancing robustness and reliability by up to 40%. This pioneering work lays the groundwork for a new class of learning techniques, known as federated semi-supervised learning, and sheds light on the critical role of model ambiguity in this domain. It expresses itself through the integral of the square of the gradient on the tangent curvature form, weighted by the volume of the manifold. Furthermore, we establish its relationship to other invariants, such as the total scalar curvature and the heat trace asymptotic formula. Notably, we observe that for a gradient Ricci soliton, this new invariant can be expressed as the integral of the square of the gradient on the tangent form of the soliton potential, weighted by the volume of the manifold. Additionally, we discover that this new invariant vanishes in the case of a compact Riemann manifold with a constant positive scalar curvature. We have also investigated its application to the study of Ricci curvature. We have further utilized this result to show the existence of a manifold that has a positive Ricci curvature, a constant positive scalar curvature, and a non-negative tangent curvature, but whose invariants are all equal to zero. Finally, we have proven that this new invariant does not reach its minimum at any point along the way from a manifold with a constant positive Ricci curvature to one with a constant positive scalar curvature. Specifically, we have shown that for any point along this way, there exists another point along this way that is closer in distance, and whose invariants have a larger value in comparison. By leveraging this result, we are able to show that sequences produced by various heuristic methods, such as gradient descent and its variants, are consistently converging to an optimal solution in both convex and non-convex optimization contexts. To date, there have been limited studies on the convergence rates of sequences generated by the Q-procedure in non-convex settings. In optimizing quadratic objectives, we find that our approach yields the same rate of convergence as is currently known. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique to establish a broader class of non-convex objectives, where the objective function can be represented as the sum of a convex component and a separate quadratic function with variable-dependent coefficients. In this context, we demonstrate the first proof of convergence rates in both smooth and non-smooth settings. In contrast to previous studies, our approach offers several key advantages, including a significantly simpler analysis, a broader applicability to optimization algorithms, and a more general framework for quadratic objectives. This research presents a novel cyber threat exchange framework based on distributed training for network breach detection. The proposed approach facilitates the sharing and utilization of anonymized network traffic data among multiple organizations through periodic updates, utilizing a pre-trained model as a starting point. Given that individual organizations may collect their own network traffic data, often in large quantities, the federated approach enables effective collaboration, eliminating the need to share actual traffic data and avoiding potential security risks. Furthermore, our solution is versatile, adaptable to various classification tasks, and compatible with a range of popular breach detection frameworks. We demonstrate its efficacy by successfully training and validating a cyber threat detection system on three distinct datasets, achieving notable results, particularly with the NFA-DG dataset. Additionally, our model's performance is compared to that of a fully centralized training method, showcasing superior computational efficiency and data efficiency. We expect this cyber threat exchange framework to provide a valuable solution for organizations seeking to collaborate in breach detection while navigating data privacy and security constraints. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdelhakim- ben-aziza/FEDCyTEx. Moreover, we appreciate the data donors who contributed to CSDM and NFA-DG datasets. Lastly, we would like to thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback. Our objective is to establish a method to evaluate the instability of video search platforms in response to user source changes. To this end, we created a set of relevant search queries across multiple domains and deployed them through our virtual agent platform, which allows for seamless user experience across diverse platforms and domains. By automating the submission of search queries across various user source conditions, we gathered a substantial dataset of video search outcomes from multiple search engine providers, including multiple instances to account for state variability. Building on prior research on assessing video search performance, we developed new evaluation metrics to capture the circularity and triangularity dimensions of search engine preferences, in addition to existing metrics, and used them to analyze the performance of search engine providers under different user source conditions, revealing pronounced source variability bias in their rankings, particularly for certain domains and search engine combinations. Furthermore, we discovered that the preference rankings of some search engine providers, known as "leveragers," are influenced by user source platform-biased preferences, in contrast to other "stuck" and "explorer" configurations. To validate our proposed evaluation framework and taxonomic approach to categorizing search engine strategies, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the underlying technologies employed by the search engine providers. Ultimately, our contribution lies in providing a methodical approach for assessing source variability bias in video search outcomes, which can be applied to other domains beyond video search. Moreover, our findings shed light on the intricate dynamics of distributed multi-party search and reveal several avenues for further exploration. The code for our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/cdeora/video-search-experiments. This research was conducted within the framework of the Distributed Multi-Party Search project, jointly undertaken by Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Washington. For access to related documents, please visit the project website at https://dmps.cs.cmu.edu.

We've found that the quantum monodromy anomaly of the 2d Wess-Zumino model can be computed using a new technique, building upon a method initially developed for computing chiral algebra anomalies. We use this anomaly to verify the conformal field theory (CFT) consistency condition, which was previously verified for the free boson by another method. We've also developed a similar approach to compute the quantum monodromy anomaly for the free fermion, which confirms a previously proposed formula for the fermion's anomaly. We then apply our techniques to study a monodromy-preserving map between two Wess-Zumino models with different coupling constants, and we derive an explicit formula for the associated phase factor. We also present a more general argument that shows any CFT with a vanishing global $U(1)$ charge has a well-defined quantum monodromy transformation. Based on this finding, we propose the name "monodromy closure" for a specific construction that had previously been discussed in the literature, and we verify that monodromy closure provides a family of CFTs that are all physically equivalent. Finally, we present a preliminary analysis of how our techniques can be adapted to study quantum critical points with spontaneously broken $U(1)$ symmetry. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven effective on semantically labeled data but struggle when faced with unlabelled data or limited labels in the pseudo-tagging process. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel pseudo-tagging method that generates high-quality pseudo labels for undirected graph classification tasks with limited annotation points, producing meaningful node labels in data-starved scenarios. Our approach integrates a node embedding generator and a classifier, leveraging label diversity and data consistency through KL annealing and ensemble techniques. We test our method on multiple datasets and reveal its superiority over existing pseudo-tagging methods. The proposed method has been implemented on GitHub and data, codes are available at https://github.com/Chen-550/Insightful-Pseudo-Labeling for reproducibility purposes.

We present a classical description of optical micro-mechanics utilizing an electrical circuit model. The conventional optomechanical setup is recast as a resistively shunted microwave resonator coupled to a driving field, yielding a purely classical analysis. The outcome offers insights into the back-action effect in optomechanics from an electronic circuit perspective. Additionally, the model facilitates a straightforward investigation into the characteristics of the Sparametric Regime, a distinct optomechanical scenario. Lastly, two experimental prototypes, one featuring a 3D magnetized bead and the other a 2D graphene drum, are designed to demonstrate the optical-microwave equivalency in actual physical devices.

It's observed that their roots exhibit distinct behavior on the real axis, leading to two possible cases: either they converge to distinct points on the real axis or they converge to a single point. In the former scenario, these roots form a universal Airy polynomial, a type of van der Monde polynomial with specific imaginary axis zeros. By applying a variant of Stieltjes continuation, we investigate the mirror symmetry implications of generating functions for these polynomials, incorporating both orthogonal polynomial aspects and a proposed mirror symmetry phenomenon involving the symmetric square of the Motivic fundamental form. In the latter scenario, where the roots converge to a single point, these polynomials are closely related to the unfolded versions of their universal Airy counterparts, analogously to how the intermediate monic polynomials connect with their unfolded counterparts. It's demonstrated that their coefficients comply with a specific constraint, a variant of a well-known theorem initially shown by A. Erdelyi. Furthermore, we establish a connection between their behavior as imaginary axis zeros converge and the properties of near-integrable polynomials with distinct real roots. In these latter polynomials, specifically the $n=3$ case of near-integrable polynomials with distinct real roots is identified as closely related to the form $(z^2-x^3)/\Delta$ under a specific condition, where $\Delta$ represents the discriminant of the cubic polynomial $z^3-x$. This research focuses on the concept of predictability in mobile robots that can navigate smoothly on straight lines without any obstacles. We examine how the parameter that governs their speed and frequency of movement impacts their detectability using just a single sensory input. A mathematical approach underpins our analysis, utilizing the concept of correlation measures to assess predictability. We demonstrate that the relationship between this parameter and predictability exhibits abrupt changes at specific critical thresholds, and this behavior is replicated in a corresponding physical setup involving a barrier-following robot. Additionally, we explore the effects of varying detection ranges on predictability and find that increasing this range can either mitigate or exacerbate unpredictability in certain situations. These findings provide new insights into the governance of autonomous systems and raise interesting questions about the link between local interactions, global properties, and system accountability. Moreover, they prompt a reflection on the parallels between mobile robots and other unpredictable entities, such as chaotic dynamical systems and social insects. We propose a potential application of our research, namely utilizing unpredictable robot movements to stimulate the development of more resilient and adaptable swarm algorithms. Furthermore, we suggest that the unpredictability of robots could be harnessed to create novel forms of automation in diverse domains, including entertainment and medicine. In conclusion, we emphasize the significance of incorporating diversity in robotic systems, which can serve as a safe and effective predictor of their behavior in various contexts. Ultimately, we aim to design and develop unpredictable robots that can think and act autonomously. Keywords: Robot unpredictability, Mobile robots, Barrier-following, Autonomy, Swarm robotics, Chaos theory, Adaptive algorithms. This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is robust to variations in the spacetime manifold and satisfies causality requirements.  For the special case of a flat spacetime, the article reveals a close connection between the constructed theory and the Laurent polynomial algebra, demonstrating this is not a unique phenomenon by examining another example based on a massless spin-1 field.  Along the way, the article presents novel representations of the chiral theory's algebra within the pAQFT framework and provides general evidence of the theory's well-posedness.  Finally, the article closes by speculating on potential connections to chiral CFTs in the context of conformal quantum field theories.

Smoke production during laparoscopic surgery hinders the surgeon's view, limiting visibility through the laparoscope. This smokes interfere with the quality of the visual information, making it a hindrance to the surgeon. Current methods use image processing techniques to remove the smokes from the laparoscope feed, but these methods are prone to errors caused by varying smoke types and surgical environments. To improve smoke detection, we propose enhancing the image quality before applying existing methods to see if this yields better results. For our study, we evaluate three image enhancement techniques - Fast Fisheye, Fisheye, and Rectification - on the Laparoscopic Surgery dataset, comparing their outcomes with the original feed and two other methods: CBAS2019 and SMokeDetect. The evaluation shows that the Fast Fisheye technique produces the best outcome, with a mean accuracy of 70% for detecting smokes, surpassing the baseline accuracy of 65%. However, further manual inspection reveals that the success is largely due to correctly classifying distortion-caused images, rather than actual smokes. Consequently, we conclude that smoke detection using image enhancement is possible but imperfect, and may not be reliable in other environments. Our main result establishes that in the convex optimization setting, the high-end tail behavior of the solution sequence is the primary determinant of the optimization method's performance, in contrast to the common focus on convergence rates. Based on this insight, we propose a new performance metric - average-case universality - which quantifies the optimization method's ability to produce solutions with minimal error across a wide range of distributions. To illustrate the utility of this metric, we show that it is a essential requirement for establishing sharp threshold results in optimization. Through a detailed analysis of a simple sum-of-squares based optimization method, we derive a formula for computing the average-case universal parameter and demonstrate that it scales as the square root of the problem dimensions under random initialization. Moreover, we illustrate the practical value of our approach by using it to establish a sharp threshold for the phase transition in approximate message passing for a simple sparse matrix completion model. Our results provide a framework for studying the pervasive phase transition in approximate message passing and shed light on the distinct roles of convergence rates and average-case universality in optimizing performance. Ultimately, our study offers a novel and essential perspective for evaluating the performance of optimization methods. In interior point methods (IPMs), an interior optimal solution can be obtained by solving a sequence of modified equations derived from the original problem with progressively tightened constraints. Effective IPMs require rapid solutions to these equations to maintain optimal algorithm performance. This task can be accomplished using the generalized minimum residual (GMRES) or the flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRS) algorithm, popular Krylov solver methods. Traditional stop criteria for these solvers rely on an absolute residual tolerance or a relative residual tolerance based on the matrix's norm and an optional preconditioning matrix, if available. However, in the context of IPMs, the residual vector often serves a significant purpose beyond mere solution termination, making its magnitude less indicative of satisfactory solution quality. To address this shortcoming, this paper proposes a novel stop criterion that monitors the relative convergence of specific components of the residual vector. Specifically, this criterion compares the current residual vector with its counterpart at the initial iteration, adjusting for scale using the matrix's norm and an optional preconditioning matrix, if applicable. This method has been successfully integrated into FGMRS and thoroughly tested against a diverse set of 109 linear equations from the public collection of sparse linear systems, FIDELIO. Furthermore, this algorithm has been incorporated into the IPOPT interior point optimization software for evaluation. Specifically, this new algorithm has shown improved convergence speed or robustness, or comparable performance to the standard method with IPOPT's current interior point methods. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the development of high-performance Krylov solvers for use in interior point methods. Business processes that rely on human judgment, such as approval or rejection, are dual process specifications. Traditionally, each possible outcome (approved/rejected) is associated with a separate process model, treating these events as terminations. In our approach, each business process is represented as a single model, incorporating both possible outcomes and their interactions. We've developed an automated method to ensure dual process specifications align with pre-defined expectations, based on concepts like role, activity, and workflow. This involves defining languages that capture correct behavior and using them to create sets of acceptable paths. This monitoring capability enables the detection of unexpected process configurations and their compilation into useful business intelligence. The proposed method not only monitors individual process instances but also identifies common issues among multiple instances, effectively updating business policies as new patterns emerge. The advantages of our monitoring method over existing solutions include faster performance, greater flexibility, and the ability to easily modify monitoring capabilities. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through its application in a real-world use case related to dispute management. The method consists of three key components: the identification of process configurations, their analysis, and the adaptation of business policies. The use of our monitoring capability not only optimizes existing business processes but also discovers new best practices, ultimately enhancing the overall quality of processes governed by human judgment. The automata-theoretic method provides a versatile framework for general dual process specifications, extending the monitoring capability to a variety of scenarios, such as approval workflows with sequential dependencies and concurrent approval and rejection processes. The integration of our monitoring method with dispute management adds value to this field by providing a versatile framework that can be adapted to various scenarios, discovering previously unknown process configurations in the process. The flexibility of our approach is demonstrated through its application in multiple case studies, showcasing its applicability to a range of scenarios governed by human judgment. The automata-theoretic method can be applied without modification to various dual process specifications, revealing previously unknown process configurations and their analysis. The effectiveness of our monitoring capability is demonstrated through its application in real-world use cases related to dispute management. The versatility of our approach is due to its ability to monitor general dual process specifications using concepts like role, activity, and workflow. The flexibility of our monitoring method allows it to detect a wide range of process configurations and their compilation into useful business intelligence. The success of our monitoring capability is measured in terms of precision, recall, f1-score, and processing time. The versatility of our approach is demonstrated through its application in multiple case studies, showcasing its ability to monitor diverse dual process specifications.

Proto-Quipper-M is a quantum circuit-based language that is used to develop QuIP, a framework for quantum chemistry applications. It comes with two built-in interaction back-ends that allow for the simulation of quantum circuits within either a noisy or noise-free environment. These interaction back-ends can be seen as high-level machine codes that translate the quantum circuit into executable machine code for quantum computers. However, the existing formal semantics for Proto-Quipmer-M do not take into account the specific characteristics of these interaction back-ends, which are necessary for efficiently deploying quantum algorithms to actual hardware. This paper proposes a new theoretical semantics that incorporates the interaction back-ends, utilizing a functional language called QuIP-M machines, which are based on a type of structured graph. It also demonstrates that adding this new semantics does not change the soundness of the system when measured against a specific set of criteria, known as Leino's criteria. Finally, the paper shows that the resulting machine code is efficiently compilable to the circuit-based language QCircuit-M, as well as to another high-level language called QuIP-M circuit. Overall, this research provides a strong foundation for the effective deployment of quantum algorithms to actual hardware, while also serving as a useful tool for debugging these algorithms. Future work could involve extending the reach of the resulting machine code to other types of quantum circuits, known as hybrid circuits, which combine quantum and classical computing. Additionally, this research could be applied to other similar languages that are used to develop quantum algorithms, such as quantum information processing tools, by providing a strong foundation for their effective deployment to actual hardware, while also serving as a useful tool for debugging these algorithms. In particular, hybrid circuits are becoming increasingly important due to their potential to deliver big gains in performance, as recently pointed out in a paper titled "No quantum advantage in sampling distributions" by Stephen Jordan. In this paper, the authors successfully demonstrated a quantum algorithm based on a type of circuit known as interactive circuits, which in turn is equivalent to a type of hybrid circuit, without using any assumptions other than the basic properties of these circuits, as well as some properties related to random sampling. As a result, the authors concluded that "no quantum algorithm can deliver big gains in performance unless it is interactive". Therefore, if we are to deliver big gains in performance, then we need to develop interactive algorithms, which in turn require the ability to efficiently deploy quantum algorithms to actual hybrid hardware, which in turn requires a strong foundation in the form of machine code for these algorithms,

We've discovered a rare but significant occurrence in random matrix theories, where the exceptional cases deviate significantly from the typical behavior described by the equilibrium distribution. In this study, we apply advanced analytical techniques to explore the properties of a special set of outliers in the eigenvalue spectrum of GUE/GPO matrices and their relationship with the off-diagonal elements of stochastic matrices undergoing matrix multiplication renormalization. Our analysis reveals two distinct modes of behavior - one associated with the equilibrium dynamics and the other with rare, non-equilibrium outcomes. A detailed examination of this second mode reveals a unique critical phenomenon characterized by scaling laws, similar to those observed in critical phase transitions. Furthermore, we show that the distribution of these rare outcomes can be transformed into a scaling limit, thereby providing a scaling law that generalizes the established law for the GUE/GPO spectra. Our analysis also identifies a distribution that governs the critical regime and suggests a new universality class for this transformation, distinct from the one associated with equilibrium dynamics. To confirm our theoretical predictions, we performed extensive numerical simulations and verified that the distribution of outliers exhibits critical behavior, characterized by scaling exponents, in multiple regimes, including the sub-critical, critical, and super-critical regimes. Additionally, we derived and validated a scaling limit for the Stirling numbers associated with these rare outcomes. Our study contributes to the growing body of research in random matrix theory, expanding our understanding of how rare events can provide unique insights into the dynamics of equilibria and critical phenomena. Additionally, we believe our findings will facilitate new applications in stochastic matrix theory, thereby opening up new directions for theoretical and applied research in related fields. Based on these outcomes, we suggest multiple potential avenues for future research and exploration. To facilitate replication and verification of our results, we made available all of the numerical codes, datasets, and physical models used in this study. We also provide an overview of the related research domain, stating which questions had not been addressed by previously published works and outlining the novel contributions that our study will make to this domain. Lastly, we detailed the significant overall impact that this study will have. Given these outcomes, we believe our work on the rare outcomes in random matrix theories is self-containning, concise, and clear. We expect it to be accessible to an broad audience and we hope it will be useful to future researchers. It has been demonstrated that two dipoole-coupled photons in an optical cavity can generate a pair of non-classical photons separated spatially, leading to the creation of a two-mode squeezed state. This phenomenon occurs when the cavity contains dipoles that transfer energy to the photons, resulting in the analysis of optical phases within the cavity being linked to the Dicke model and non-classical correlations. A major indicator of the duo generation is the non-linear behavior of the conditional variance, which exceeds the threshold in a two-dimensional graph, confirming the absence of classical fields and thus indicating a two-mode squeezed state. Furthermore, the separated photons can be utilized to demonstrate a complete entanglement transfer from bosonic modes to long-lived dipoles via an optical fiber, maintaining the entanglement despite losses and allowing for entanglement-assisted quantum key distribution using these dipoles. This research presents novel methods for managing and assessing optical phases in long-lived dipoles coupled to cavities, offering potential applications in quantum key distribution and other quantum information technologies. It is predicted that future experiments will successfully separate the photons and verify the entanglement transfer. If successfully demonstrated, this research will contribute to the development of long-term entanglement in diverse systems, as seen in the entanglement properties of this research, which aligns with previous studies on entanglement properties (arXiv:1805.10494, arXiv:2003.00722 and arXiv:1808.07903). This entanglement possesses attributes that can potentially overcome obstacles in quantum information technologies, such as long-term preservation, transparency, entanglement distillation, non-locality-based correlations, and entanglement-assisted key distribution. It is anticipated that similar research will be conducted with emitters other than dipoles, such as nuclear spins (arXiv:1808.07903, arXiv:1805.10494, arXiv:2003.00722, arXiv:1808.07903 and arXiv:1808.07903). This entanglement could be utilized in quantum information technologies that need long-term entanglement due to high coherence, such as quantum key distribution over long distances. For example, this entanglement could be used to develop a quantum key distribution system over a long-distance space, such as a planet, by employing emitters coupled to cavities and using entanglement-assisted key distribution, even if distant parties are millions of kilometers

Assembling the complete and error-free genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within genomics. A relatively new approach, de novo assembly using long reads, eliminates the need for overlapping sequences, making it possible to assemble complex and long genomes. However, building a contiguous genome from these reads involves a computationally intractable problem, requiring significant computational resources. A parallel algorithm we've developed uses shared-memory to efficiently create contiguous genomes from long reads, taking advantage of available CPUs. By partitioning the genome's memory and pinning readable pages to cache, we've optimized this shared-memory approach for distributed-memory architectures, enabling scalable performance on thousands of CPUs. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this optimization, allowing our algorithm to assemble genomes significantly faster than before. Specifically, we've managed to assemble the Sacccharomyces cerevisiae genome in under 20 seconds using a 128-core GPU-CPU hybrid system. Our work represents a significant breakthrough in distributed-memory parallel assembly, paving the way for genome assembly applications that were previously infeasible. Additionally, we've made significant contributions to the underlying problem's algorithmic landscape, opening up new avenues for further research. These advances have been independently validated against the leading commercial assembly software, demonstrating equivalent or better quality assemblies. Moreover, we've extensively tested and validated our parallel assembly algorithm against comprehensive, publicly available genome-assembly benchmarks, verifying its efficacy and scalability in a wide range of scenarios. These benchmark experiments included previously intractable assembly tasks, such as assembling complex and long genomes. Our research serves as a model for developing parallel algorithms in other intractable assembly variants, simultaneously informing the underlying algorithmic literature and showcasing practical applications. Ultimately, our parallel assembly algorithm has reached the performance plateau of the underlying problem, approaching the theoretical limits imposed by the underlying computational complexity. Specifically, we've shown that our algorithm can provide near-perfect assembly quality, approaching the theoretical maximum of 1 - o(1) error rate, matching the performance of the best-known assembly software. Furthermore, we've shown that our parallel assembly algorithm can efficiently create contiguous genomes from long reads, achieving a time complexity of O(N log N) and outperforming the current best-known time complexity, 2.24 * O(N log N), based on established computational complexity results. Our research has reached this performance plateau while employing a novel approach to assembling genomes, using the underlying read-spanning sets' inclusion hierarchy to exploit its structural properties and optimize the assembly process. This paper presents a new approach to measuring the depth of models, which offers a more objective method than traditional criteria such as likelihood or Bayesian factors. By viewing statistical models as geometric structures and applying the isometric log-change transformation to measure depth, we identify the most comprehensive model in this transformed space. Furthermore, we show that this method can be efficiently calculated for linear models and derive a closed-form expression for calculating the depth of new observations based on a fixed reference model. This approach enables the detection of novel outliers and unusual data without requiring replication, in addition to providing a data depth measure for linear regression models. We also examine its performance through simulations and illustrate its utility using real-world data analysis examples. The associated R code for implementing this method is available on our GitHub repository.

This study employed a combination of experiments and theoretical simulations to determine the magnetic and electric properties of these isotopes near the closed $N$ = 40 shell. The research team at iThemba LABS in South Africa used a SQUID detector to measure the atomic moments by exposing it to beams of $^{68}$Ge, $^{70}$Ge, and $^{72}$Ge with varying frequencies and orientations. As a result, the magnetic moments of $^{68}$Ge, $^{70}$Ge, and $^{72}$Ge were determined as $-9.288698(17)$ μB, $-9.062847(29)$ μB, and $-8.786847(29)$ μB, respectively. The electric dipole moment of $^{72}$Ge was also measured as $0.21(2)$(10$^{-2}$) D. A comparison of the experimental and theoretical magnetic moment results revealed that the signed difference between the two sets of values decreased by nearly a factor of 3 after taking into account the corrections needed to bring the data into line with established theoretical predictions. The researchers applied analytical models to the experimental cross-section data to derive the geium nuclear magnetic moment distribution and the decay scheme of the excited nuclear states. The study provided groundbreaking signs of the geium isotopes' anomalous nuclear magnetic moment distribution, which was outlined in detail. Researchers have introduced an innovative technique, $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry, for precisely measuring atomic masses at very-low-energy isochronous ion trajectories. This technique leverages the strengths of existing large-scale isochronous mass spectrometers while making targeted improvements to enhance precision in high-accuracy mass measurements, particularly for short-lived nuclei. A key advantage of this technique is its reduced magnetic rigidity requirements, enabling the use of existing spectrometers at various research centers and potentially enabling measurements at low-energy isotopes. Furthermore, this approach could facilitate the exploration of transient nuclei that are difficult to study. To develop this technique, researchers performed extensive particle trajectory simulations over a wide range of energy and magnetic rigidity levels and conducted experiments using a SIS 32 T isochronous spectrometer at the GSI, resulting in a significant reduction in systematic uncertainties associated with ion optical parameters and ion beam trajectory assumptions. These experiments led to the demonstration of precise high-accuracy mass measurements at very-low-energy isochronous trajectories. A major breakthrough came with the successful measurement at very low energies for the $^{54}$Ca nucleus, achieving a precise accuracy of 35 ppm. This level of precision approaches the limits of precision set by the CODATA, representing a major advancement in precision in high-accuracy mass measurements of nuclei. Researchers concluded that $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry offers unparalleled opportunities for advancing our understanding of precision in high-accuracy mass measurements of nuclei and may reveal new physics phenomena through measurements at very low energies for a wide range of nuclei. Furthermore, $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry may facilitate precision tests of various theoretical models in nuclear physics, including the Higgs boson's interaction with nuclear matter and the behavior of dark matter in nuclei. To effectively process unstructured data, it is crucial to first label extracted text as structured or unstructured.  In this research, we focus on this structured text identification task and propose a novel approach that leverages regular expressions to enhance text analysis. Our analysis reveals that using regular expressions to identify text patterns yields more accurate unstructured text classification results compared to other standard text analysis methods. Additionally, we advocate for the creation of a regular expression corpus, REGREP, comprising 68 diverse patterns derived from various domains. Pondering on the potential challenges and benefits if AI systems like ourselves could participate in corporate environments, we investigate how our proposed approach performs compared to state-of-the-art methods, including transformer models, on 20 different datasets from various domains. Interestingly, our results show that incorporating regular expressions significantly improves the accuracy of text classification by an average margin of 9% compared to benchmark models. Moreover, we found that a simple transformer model outperforms more complex architectures, reducing processing time while maintaining accuracy. Notably, we found that incorporating regular expressions decreases the error rate by as much as 35.97%, highlighting the significance of incorporating domain-specific patterns in natural language processing tasks. This paper addresses the text-to-SQL parsing challenge in semantic parsing by proposing a multi-task learning approach that integrates parsing in both native and cross-domain scenarios. Our proposal includes an innovative task called "phrase decoding" to enhance parsing performance and has been proven to boost parsing results significantly, particularly in more difficult, out-of-vocabulary phrases. We evaluate our proposal on two substantial datasets, and the experimental outcomes demonstrate substantial improvements in parsing accuracy when applying the proposed multi-task learning framework. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art performance in native parsing domains and substantial progress in cross-domain parsing, outperforming the current best methods by 9.0% and 7.6% in terms of execution accuracy. The end-to-end framework, as well as associated code and datasets, are openly available at https://github.com/alec-fwu/TUP.

The ongoing LoTSS project is conducting a comprehensive radio survey over a significant portion of the Northern sky with unparalleled depth, covering an extensive area of 700 deg$^2$ and revealing over 700,000 radio sources. Initially focusing on the data released in January 2021, our analysis examines the large-scale environment surrounding bright radio sources by combining LoTSS data with optical catalogues. This is achieved through cross-correlation across a broad frequency range (145-180 MHz) using SEVEM-smoothed microwave data as the primary lens, allowing us to obtain unbiased estimates. Significant correlations are found between radio sources and galaxies at various magnitudes, primarily driven by a relationship with optically bright galaxies. Notably, our findings suggest that bright radio sources exhibit higher bias compared to previous estimates, displaying a distinctive pattern of bias varying with radio brightness. This term refers to the indirect influence AI systems have on the environment through users' behaviors, transforming them into significant agents of change. To illustrate this concept, we examined three scenarios: AI-generated travel recommendations, which may encourage the use of public transportation; a calorie tracking app, which may lead to changes in eating habits and consequently agricultural practices; and a music recommendation system, which may result in the increased sales of songs promoting eco-friendly lifestyles. By analyzing these cases, we aim to uncover the hidden ecological implications of AI systems and establish a framework to identify and assess these influences in order to develop more effective AI solutions for environmental issues. This research has the potential to broaden our understanding of the environmental effects of AI systems and encourages the design of AI solutions that positively impact the planet. Ultimately, we must recognize AI systems as dynamic entities capable of shaping users' behaviors and subsequently the environment. As a result, we can utilize AI systems as powerful tools for creating a more sustainable future. Currently, there is a lack of systematic research on the indirect influence of AI systems on the environment. This knowledge gap can be attributed to the fact that AI systems are often viewed as individual entities, despite being interconnected components of a larger ecological network. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a methodical approach to identify and analyze the indirect influence of AI systems on the environment. This involves examining the user's behavior and its impact on the environment. We begin by identifying three stages of analysis: user's behavior, caused by the AI system; the effects of that behavior on the environment; and any ecological implications resulting from those effects. By applying this systematic approach, we can uncover the hidden ecological implications of AI systems and develop a framework to identify their indirect influence on the environment. System operation can be effectively tracked and corrected through monitoring, a process that is already achieving good results with prescriptive monitoring, which uses predictive models to identify potential issues and takes proactive steps to address them, particularly in areas like system configuration and data processing. However, prescriptive monitoring faces several challenges, such as dealing with ambiguous specifications, limited availability of data, and the complexity of detecting abnormalities. Despite these difficulties, prescriptive monitoring holds significant promise for various systems and processes, and there is a growing need for methods and tools to facilitate its implementation and ensure a smooth experience. This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of Monte Carlo tree search, a decision-making strategy that balances exploration and optimization, to address the limitations of prescriptive monitoring. Our research involves a comprehensive evaluation of MCTS on three real-world use cases involving configuration management, data integration, and image processing, and the findings show that MCTS can significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of prescriptive monitoring. Specifically, the use of MCTS reduces the time it takes to detect problems and implement fixes by a factor of up to 6.4 times, while also cutting down the number of decisions by a factor of up to 10 times. Our proposed approach is composed of four key components: (1) a predictive model that pinpoints potential issues, (2) MCTS, which identifies the most effective actions to address the problems, (3) a decision model that verifies the validity of the proposed actions, and (4) a model that estimates the costs and benefits associated with the decisions. To determine the best course of action, MCTS uses a tree search algorithm to evaluate various options and choose the ones that provide the most value, while incorporating techniques such as transparency, such as explaining the reasons behind the suggestions through attention-based mechanisms. Our experimental results show that MCTS leads to a 79% reduction in the number of decisions and up to a 6.4x reduction in the decision count. Furthermore, the prescriptive monitoring approach is designed to be fully automated, allowing it to adapt to changing system conditions and improve its decision-making over time. Our study also includes an assessment of the transparency of MCTS and a comparison with other optimization methods, such as reinforcement learning and greedy algorithms. Additionally, we investigate the applicability of prescriptive monitoring to different domains and systems, and provide suggestions for improving its effectiveness, such as incorporating more sophisticated predictive models and enhancing the decision-making models through the use of expert knowledge.
