To expand this framework, we've developed a generalized Boussinesq model that includes the Magneto-Hydrodynamic dynamics and purchases of chemical reactions within the fluid. The model's governing equations are complemented by stabilization techniques to ensure numerical stability. The application of the finite element method and conjugate gradient solver follows standard practices. Instead of limiting the control to a single goal, we utilize the finite element method to control multiple objectives simultaneously, leveraging the residual-based approach for stabilization. We've tested the methodology on two diverse scenarios: the first involves the free convection of a binary mixture near its critical temperature, and the second is the magnetohydrodynamic convection of a binary mixture in a rotating cylinder. The stability and performance of our approach are compared with traditional fixed goal methods, revealing significant improvements in numerical stability for complex magnetohydrodynamic convection problems. The methodology's versatility and adaptability have been demonstrated, and it is anticipated that these results will be extended to other problem types. Building upon the success of Parameterized Complexity, which examines how to manage hard problems by using limited resources, the Kernelization framework aims to reduce the size and complexity of intractable problems while preserving their parameters. This study focuses on Stacking Problems (SP) – a class of problems that involve determining if a set of objects can be stacked on top of one another – and investigates kernelization for these problems. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to existing insights, no general kernelization exists for SP. Instead, we define a new class of super-stacking problems (SSP) and demonstrate that kernelization is possible for SSP with constraints. These findings offer valuable guidance for classifying complex problems within the context of Stacking Problems and super-stacking problems. Furthermore, our work introduces novel applications of stacking problems in combinatorial geometry, establishing connections between these problems and established results in the field. Lastly, we explore potential avenues for future research, including extending our results to more general problem classes, such as Makanai-Fajiclass problems. Additionally, we conjecture the absence of kernelization for a specific class of problems involving geometric arrangements.

In certain situations, particularly in social networks, individuals may seek to gain an advantage by adopting the views held by others, as this can provide a sense of security and confidence in their choices. This study examines how social connections become established in a scenario where individuals have different perspectives, as the dynamics of this process lead to an equilibrium where each person holds a unique view. We explore two methods for evaluating the certainty individuals have in their choices: one focuses on the structure of social relationships and the other considers the distribution of views within the network. Both approaches are challenging to quantify, so we establish a framework for making approximate assessments based on a network's core components and the distribution of views. This framework offers a practical method for obtaining limited assurance about the certainty of choices in a wide range of scenarios. To illustrate our findings, we use two examples: one involving a star-shaped network and another with a more complex structure. In both cases, we demonstrate how the framework can provide a lower bound for measuring the certainty of choices. Interestingly, this bound relies heavily on the network's core components and is resistant to changes in its edges. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of epistemic modal logic in representing and processing uncertainty in networks. By integrating this approach with existing research on structural equilibrium, we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between social relationships and the distribution of views. This combined knowledge enables us to establish a link between the certainty of choices and the network's core components. In particular, we show that the lowest level of certainty can be achieved when a network is completely disconnected. We hope that this study will contribute to the development of new approaches for evaluating the certainty of choices in social networks and the design of more effective algorithms for making approximate assessments. Using cutting-edge simulation methods, we analyzed how genes are transcribed in human cells, revealing that some genes take time to start producing RNA while others are quickly active. We developed an approach to identify and understand the reasons behind the varying speeds of transcriptional activation across different genes. Notably, we found that genes with delayed transcriptional responses are more likely to include sequences that can bind multiple transcription factors, which hinders the transcription process. Conversely, genes with rapid transcriptional activation tend to lack these inhibitory sequences. By integrating our findings with existing data on chromatin modifications, we uncovered a potential causal relationship, suggesting that certain histone modifications can prevent the binding of transcription factors to suppressive sequences, thereby facilitating transcriptional activation. Our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between DNA sequences, transcription factors, and chromatin modifications that influence gene expression in human cells. Additionally, we have made public the software tools used in this study that enable the simulation of transcriptional dynamics based on sequences. With a focus on SU(N) theories where fermions belong to odd representations, we explore various theories and their proposed duals, examining the existing literature and identifying potential avenues for supersymmetric dualities. By analyzing a spectrum of flavored deformations and Spencer duals, we establish non-supersymmetric counterparts for SU(N) theories across multiple odd-dimensional irregularities. We also introduce novel duals for SU(N) theories involving fermions in (N+1)-dimensional, (2N+1)-dimensional, and 2N+1-dimensional irregularities, along with a Spencer dual for SU(N) theory with a 4-dimensional Fermi multiplet. We further extend our research to χSB region for SU(N) theories involving 3, 5, and 7-dimensional irregularities and propose non-supersymmetric duals for χSB theories, incorporating both chiral and recentering twists. We also discuss the center symmetry in these theories, examining the impact of duals and twists on this aspect. Lastly, we briefly explore duals for Sp(N) and SO(N) chiral gauge theories, highlighting the distinct features and differences that arise due to the distinct nature of Sp(N) and SO(N) theories, coupled with an overview of potential research directions in this domain. A linear complementary set of group codes is defined as a collection of group codes with identical cyclic codes and ranks that differ by one, existing within the same finite principal ideal domain and indexed by distinct elements of a group. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of linear complementary sets of group codes through the study of multiplicative subgroup polynomials. Specifically, if a polynomial's Galois conjugates cover all elements of a finite cyclic group except for one, we demonstrate that it cannot be expressed as a multiplicative subgroup polynomial unless its coefficients have a specific recursive property. Moreover, we prove that such a polynomial does in fact generate the Galois field if and only if its coefficients meet this particular recursive criterion, thus resolving a long-standing open problem. As a direct result, the existence of linear complementary sets for group codes is comprehensively studied and fully characterized based on the order of the underlying group. Additionally, we provide two explicit examples of linear complementary sets for abelian groups indexed by $\mathbb{Z}_n \times \mathbb{Z}_m$ when both $n$ and $m$ are greater than two, filling a notable gap in existing research. Ultimately, the study of linear complementary sets for group codes is poised to contribute significantly to the broader field of coding theory. We hope that our work will inspire the creation of more innovative coding schemes using linear complementary sets, thereby driving progress in the field. We intend to explore this potential more fully in a companion paper. We have also taken this opportunity to clarify and rectify certain errors and ambiguities present in an earlier publication, bringing the text up to date in terms of accuracy and completeness. We analyze the dynamics of complex fluids confined to channels with irregularities, investigating how channel surface details influence flow behavior in shear-thickening and shear-thinning fluids. By utilizing a stochastic framework for studying shear-induced particle movements, we explore the global effects of surface geometrical characteristics on flow behavior and establish a scaling relationship linking fluid response to local surface features and the fluid's rheological properties. This scaling relationship enables us to classify the flow dynamics based on a dimensionless group, which distinguates shear-thickening and shear-thinning behaviors for complex fluids. Moreover, our study reveals that shear-thickening fluids are generally more susceptible to flow disruptions due to channel surface irregularities, whereas shear-thinning fluids tend to be less affected. Our proposed scaling approach provides a universal framework for evaluating the impact of surface roughness on fluid dynamics and aids in predicting flow behavior and its implications in designing complex fluid-based technologies. Furthermore, our study discuses the practical significance of surface roughness in the flow dynamics of shear-thickening and shear-thinning fluids, highlighting the importance of accurate surface characterization and dimensional analysis for predicting flow phenomena. Ultimately, our work lays a foundational understanding of the intricate interplay between surface roughness, fluid rheology, and flow behavior, paving the way for further exploration of this intriguing phenomenon. Additionally, our study points to potential applications in engineering that involve designing flows with specific characteristics using surfaces with tailored roughness, thus potentially yielding notable practical benefits. Conversely, our study also touches upon potential drawbacks related to flow disruptions that might arise due to channel surface irregularities, which could have significant implications for fluid dynamics and flow engineering. To address these concerns, our work offers a universal framework for evaluating and controlling flow behavior and its implications in designing complex fluid-based technologies. Furthermore, our study could aid in developing methods for characterizing surface roughness and its effects on fluid dynamics, thus providing practical insights for flow engineering and design. To effectively address a power crisis, a strategic approach is necessary to analyze and understand consumer behavior, particularly how their energy consumption varies throughout the day. This analysis enables utilities to target specific hours when demand is high and implement time-of-use pricing, educating customers and motivating them to shift their usage to off-peak hours. To that end, this research aims to develop a statistical model that can accurately predict hourly electricity usage with minimal error. In the context of a power crisis, this model will help utilities identify critical hours, identify the driving factors behind high energy consumption, and utilize the results to inform pricing policies and demand response strategies. Utilizing real-world data from the Southeastern Electricity Authority of Nigeria, this study proposes a statistical model that leverages Trend Analysis and Seasonal Decomposition to forecast electricity usage. Noting that historical consumption patterns can predict future usage with some degree of accuracy, this model does not account for future changes in consumer behavior. Nonetheless, when constrained to the available data, this approach delivers a forecasting error rate of 5.64%, surpassing the baseline forecasting method that incorporates seasonal patterns alone, which yields an error rate of 8.74%. Ultimately, this research validates the efficacy of statistical modeling in forecasting hourly electricity usage, providing insights into consumer behavior and guiding decision-making at utilities. Customized search results can skew internet research by favoring established sources over new information, including academic studies. This bias may cause researchers to overlook relevant data, such as studies listed in the National Center for Biotechnology Information's database. We investigated the influence of customized search by examining how it affects the discovery of existing studies focusing on chatterbots and uncovers the underlying psychological and social factors contributing to this phenomenon. We applied the concepts of self-categorization theory and social identity theory to explain the behaviors of Google's algorithms and its potential consequences. We also developed and tested a method for detecting customized search bias, which can be applied to various research fields. Our study's results show that approximately 70% of relevant Google search results fail to include pertinent information from the National Center for Biotechnology Information's database. We identified several underlying factors contributing to this bias, including users' search terms, the quantity of relevant information, and users' underlying psychological and social motivations. These factors highlight the complexities of customized search and its potential impacts on different research fields. Our study's findings suggest that researchers may overlook crucial information when relying on customized search results, and we provide potential solutions for mitigating this bias, including the use of diverse search engines and the application of pre-filtering methods. Automatically creating code from visual representations is a long-standing challenge in software research. Recent breakthroughs using graph neural networks have made significant progress in tackling this problem, though flow diagrams present an obstacle due to their disjointed structure, multiple node types, and often ambiguous labels. We introduce GRCNN, a novel end-to-end neural network capable of recognizing and translating flow diagrams into programs. Leveraging a unique graph recognition convolutional neural network (GRCNN), GRCNN can differentiate between varied diagram types, including control flow diagrams with no branches, and even complex diagrams involving loops and multiple branches. We have tested GRCNN on over 1800 program-flow diagram pairs to demonstrate its effectiveness, achieving a 97% accuracy in recognizing diagram types and a 99% accuracy in translating programs, further validating the efficacy of our approach with a successful deployment in the BlockModeling tool. Despite its remarkable performance, GRCNN's translation precision slightly declines on more intricate control flow diagrams with branches and loops, however, it exhibits robust consistency across multiple experts and is versatile in capturing various diagram types. Furthermore, we have found that its node and edge representation results exhibit substantial similarity to expert annotations, thereby presenting a valuable form of program analysis. We envision this research to have far-reaching implications in the field of program understanding, software maintenance, and related areas. To conclude, GRCNN presents an innovative and highly effective solution for the intricate task of general program synthesis. The exoplanet desert around medium to high-mass stars is well established, characterised by a significant challenge in discovering planets with masses similar to Saturn's due to limitations in current detection methods and our understanding of exoplanet formation and migration. The main goal of this study is to verify the presence of this desert around lower mass stars (less than 10 solar masses) using a large dataset containing over 500 planets discovered by HARPS and additional CORALIE observations. The study uses a statistical analysis to compare the mass distribution of Saturn-mass exoplanets in relation to sub-Saturn-mass exoplanets in the detected sample, and considers several detection biases in the analysis. The result shows that there is no evident "desert" around lower mass stars, and the mass distribution of discovered exoplanets is consistent with a uniform mass ratio, contradicting previous studies that suggested a significant detection bias in the low-mass range. The study's findings will be valuable in understanding exoplanet formation and migration theories, and may aid in the development of more accurate statistical population models for exoplanet discovery in future studies. By examining nilpotent algebras in prime degree, we gain insight into their behavior and its relationship with the curve's differential equations, ultimately allowing for a full classification in this context. We reevaluate the process of global averaging in light of optimal transport theory. Our approach is to treat the averaging procedure as a mass conservation challenge, solved through solutions to an optimal transport problem. By applying properties of minimal transports, we demonstrate that solutions to this problem provide a clear geometric interpretation of global averaging in features and representational spaces. In addition, we show that the averaging procedure can be represented as a form of regularization in the context of optimal transport. Our methodology enables the computation of global averages in high-dimensional scenarios with reduced computational requirements. We also extend the concept of global averaging to accommodate outliers through innovations in optimal transport theory, specifically the use of a generalized kinetic energy metric. We test our methods in a range of applications, including the analysis of global features in high-dimensional images and the detection of anomalies in time series data. The source code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/fseguin/global-averaging. The PyTorch 1.9.0 version of the code can also be found on the VisionLab website at http://visionlab.org/global-averaging.

Recently, depth assessment has emerged as a promising method for improving the performance of pre-trained models.  In this study, we examined the effectiveness of depth assessment, comparing it to classification-based pre-training for semantic segmentation.  Through extensive analysis of the role of pre-training targets in the success of these approaches, we gained valuable insights.  Our findings suggest that classification-based pre-training outperforms depth assessment in various scenarios, making it a more reliable choice for the task of semantic segmentation.  Additionally, our study provides a detailed understanding of the connection between pre-training targets and the success of pre-trained models, a valuable area of research that future scholars can explore. Developing natural language processing systems that can effectively create and manipulate time-series data is crucial for various applications, yet generating coherent and interesting time-series data remains an unsolved problem in the field. Current approaches relying on sequential neural models fall short due to their focus on either narrative structure or temporal relationships. To address this gap, we present TCube, a novel sequence-to-sequence model that seamlessly integrates temporal information and narrative structure alongside a domain-agnostic feature set. TCube utilizes the FastText library to capture significant temporal patterns and incorporates attention mechanisms to enhance the modeling of temporal relationships within time-series data. Additionally, it employs a structured narrative template to guide the generation of coherent and interesting time-series data. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of TCube in modeling temporal relationships and narrative structure. Furthermore, generated time-series data examined by human annotators showed high preferences for TCube. The source code for TCube is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jjwang1122/TCube for public access.

This study delves into users' external link sharing behavior on Stack Overflow to gain insights into how they utilize the platform for information dissemination. By analyzing associated factors, such as shared content types and users' professional activities, the research provides valuable knowledge on how Stack Overflow users propagate knowledge externally via linked resources. The investigation addresses a pressing query regarding whether Stack Overflow users engage in propagating knowledge externally via external links and investigates the relationship between shared external links and users' professional activities, as well as other relevant factors. The findings could contribute to the development of features that support knowledge dissemination, ultimately enhancing users' overall experience on the platform. The research methodology involves collecting a non-random sample of question IDs from users with at least 10 reputation points and associated external links, totaling 1,412,382 entries. Each item was then analyzed manually to gather detailed information on shared content, users' tags, and other related metadata. To identify users' professional connections, the research utilizes data from LinkedIn, employing the BigGraph framework to establish connections between the two platforms. The study's analysis yields several significant outcomes, revealing that Stack Overflow users frequently share various types of external links, including knowledge bases, blogs, and academic resources, often related to users' professional activities in data science and software development. Interestingly, the research discovers that users who share knowledge externally via external links are more likely to engage in other propagating activities, such as commenting and editing, on the platform. Furthermore, the study finds a positive correlation between users' reputation points and their external link sharing behavior, as well as other professional activities on Stack Overflow. Ultimately, the research concludes that Stack Overflow users do engage in propagating knowledge externally via external links and that such behavior is diverse in terms of content types and users' professional activities. Based on these findings, the study suggests several features that could support knowledge dissemination on the platform, including a knowledge dissemination reward system and a comprehensive knowledge graph to connect dispersed knowledge resources. The research provides various opportunities for further investigation, such as investigating the relationship between users' external link sharing behavior and other professional activities on Stack Overflow. Additionally, the study could be replicated on other platforms to confirm whether the observed patterns are unique to Stack Overflow or more broadly applicable across the internet. In computer systems, energy efficiency is a critical factor that determines processor performance, whether it's a desktop, laptop, or mobile device, greatly influenced by how well the Central Processing Unit coordinates tasks. Efficient task management with minimal resource waste is therefore a key challenge in designing architectures, where the quality of the task scheduling directly impacts processor energy consumption and performance. Inspired by the potential of neuromorphic computing in parallel processing, this research proposes a novel task allocation algorithm using spiking neural networks, ensuring high precision and optimal energy efficiency by generating multiple task assignment solutions, then selecting the best fit based on task duration and available resources, thus preventing unnecessary resource usage and energy waste. The tasks are modeled as neurons with firing thresholds and spike durations, where a task requires less resources than another, leading to a lower firing threshold and shorter spike duration. The proposed algorithm accurately identifies suitable task assignments and generates minimal waste, where a flexible architecture with multiple task dependencies is also designed to simulate nested tasks, where a parent task needs to complete before its child task can begin. Experimental results show the algorithm achieves near-perfect task assignment accuracy and minimal task scheduling latency, while also reducing energy consumption by limiting resource usage and task switching, ultimately achieving up to 98.5% reduction in average energy consumption and 89.1% reduction in average resource overuse. The research introduces novel enhancements, where a revised architecture with flexible task duration modeling is introduced, where task duration is modeled as a binomial distribution, leading to further improved performance and more accurate results. The Spiking Task Assignment algorithm is later converted into hardware, where the performance under various VLSI constraints is evaluated, demonstrating robustness and energy efficiency under different constraint scenarios. The conversion to hardware involves mapping the algorithm to a Crossbar-based Neuromorphic Core Cell Array, where task firing thresholds and spike durations are configured through the selection of suitable weights and spike strengths, to achieve optimal energy efficiency and precise task assignment. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of quark stars composed primarily of spin-aligned strange quarks under the influence of intense magnetic fields. We employed the MIT bag model and considered the effects of magnetic fields on quark matter using the relativistic mean field theory. Our study involves calculating thermodynamic properties such as specific heat, magnetic free energy, and entropy within the context of the relativistic Stefan-Boltzmann model. Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of magnetic fields, temperature, and strange quark potential on the mass-radius radius of quark stars. Our findings demonstrate that, in the presence of magnetic fields and elevated temperatures, quark stars undergo significant radial changes, potentially resulting from phase transitions or changes in their constituent quark matter. This behavior is akin to that observed in neutron stars under similar conditions. Additionally, we note that the mass-radius radius of spin-aligned strange quark star could be expanded into a double-valued function in relation to the magnetic field strength. This behavior is an uncommon phenomenon in compact stars. In contrast, in the absence of magnetic fields, quark stars exhibit minimal radial changes in response to temperature or other internal modifications. This is notably similar to the observed characteristics of isolated neutron star in the PSR J1713+3949. Lastly, our research indicates that intense magnetic fields can induce significant alterations in the mass-radius radius of quark stars, potentially resulting from changes in their internal spin alignment or thermal properties. This understanding may hold key implications for the ongoing observation and analysis of quark stars and compact objects in radio and X-ray spectra. It could also provide valuable insights into their internal microphysics and the inherent qualities of free strange quarks. Ultimately, shedding light on the uncertainties surrounding the theoretical mass-radius radius of isolated quark stars. This research explores how nonlinear identification involving eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be estimated dynamically, using a new approach based on a minimal rational interpolation method that doesn't require any prior knowledge of eigenvalues or eigenvectors. Unlike previous interpolation methods that rely on linear mappings, this novel approach handles complex nonlinear relationships and can effectively cope with noisy data. Following a comprehensive theoretical analysis, we develop a practical algorithm for the dynamic estimation of nonlinear eigensystems and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations involving two case studies, one simulation-based and the other using real data from a study on brain activity. This latter application reveals that the proposed method can provide an accurate and stable estimation of the nonlinear eigensystem, outperforming a comparison method that uses a least-squares based approach. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of noise on the estimated eigenvalues and eigenvectors in a number of Monte Carlo experiments. In all cases, the proposed algorithm shows promising results, making it a viable option for a wide range of applications involving nonlinear eigensystems. Additionally, the associated software is freely available upon request to the author. Certain types of nuclear transitions known as $\beta$-transitions are characterized by the number of neutrons minus protons remaining constant, and their occurrence is influenced by the presence of an energy barrier, called the $T=0$ or $T=1$ gap, which hinders certain transitions. When the barrier is overcome, the excess energy is divided fairly among the created neutrons and protons, resulting in a higher excitation energy than would be possible if the excess energy were absorbed by a single particle, leading to "greedy" transitions. This concept can explain the existence of "direct" and "indirect" transitions, as well as "two-step" transitions, and it also provides a simplified understanding of the role of multinucleon condensates in heavy nuclei, as documented in the 2021 review article by Simpson and Mavraganis. It is also proposed that multinucleon condensates, such as short-range correlations, could further lower the energy barrier and facilitate "intermediate" transitions that fall between direct and indirect two-step transitions. These intermediate transitions are expected to be more prevalent at lower energies and excitations and involve nuclei with smaller mass differences, such as $A\sim 30-60$. Furthermore, it is anticipated that these intermediate transitions will be masked by background two-step transitions and are thus awaiting the development of precise experimental measurement capabilities to be empirically verified. If confirmed, it is hypothesized that these intermediate transitions will be a significant aspect of $\beta$-transitions and play a crucial role in understanding the dynamics of nearby nuclei. It is also suggested that these intermediate transitions could be mirrored by "inverse $\beta$-transfers", which are currently difficult to measure directly but may become more accessible with the development of precision spectroscopy using the laser electron photon sphere experiment at Jefferson Lab. In conclusion, the proposed classification of greedy $\beta$-transitions provides a straightforward and intuitive understanding of the occurrence of direct, indirect, and two-step transitions and predicts the existence of intermediate transitions that fall between direct and indirect two-step transitions and are anticipated to be empirically verified. Additionally, it is hypothesized that these intermediate transitions will be a significant aspect of $\beta$-transitions and play a crucial role in understanding the local nuclear dynamics. Unlike other clarity tools, this method can analyze complex models with numerous inputs and outputs. Recent advancements in Trusted Execution Environments have made it possible to execute code in a secure manner, however, this has yet to translate to a comprehensive solution for secure machine learning. The lack of a unified framework has led to a disjointed approach, with proposals oversimplifying complex issues or imposing undue restrictions on model structure. This paper introduces Flatee, a novel framework that integrates TEEs with graph neural networks to create a more cohesive solution for secure machine learning. By focusing on cross-enclave communication, Flatee facilitates the collaboration of multiple models across different TEEs, thereby addressing a critical gap in previous research. Furthermore, Flatee's approach enables the secure deployment of models on remote cloud infrastructure, subject to strict compliance with Cloudflare's memory constraints. The results demonstrate that Flatee can successfully train models on various datasets, achieving accuracy rates comparable to standard ML models, while remaining fully compliant with Cuckooz and WEEVE standards. Moreover, Flatee's performance is unaffected by communication costs, with model training times comparable to conventional ML methods. Ultimately, Flatee embodies a comprehensive solution for secure machine learning, meeting the stringent requirements of high-stakes applications. We introduce "random model predictive regulation" (RMPR), an extension of the random model predictive control (R MPC) concept, which adapts model predictive control methods to operate in regulatory modes. RMPR enables the direct generation of control inputs and feedback policies from state observations, facilitating the tracking of reference signals in systems with nonlinear dynamics and constraints. Building upon the mathematical framework of optimal transport, RMPR is formulated as an optimization problem and is computationally efficient, producing feasible outcomes within acceptable computational times. In this paper, we demonstrate RMPR using a simple aircraft flight control system and evaluate its performance using simulation scenarios. The results show that RMPR successfully tracks a variety of reference signals in a safety-critical environment, outperforming baseline control methods. The computational complexity of RMPR was found to be directly proportional to the square of the discrete time step, making it suitable for real-time high-speed processing. The code used in this research is publicly accessible, allowing for the reproduction of results and future advancements in the field. Furthermore, RMPR possesses inherent robustness and safety features, which can be exploited in the design of flight control systems. The approach presented in this paper serves as a starting point for developing control methods that incorporate performance, robustness, and safety constraints into regulatory systems. The integration of RMPR with constraints is an area of ongoing research, which may involve the use of graph theory, constraint relaxation, and other optimization techniques. The mathematical framework of RMPR is a key area of focus and can be further developed through the application of advanced mathematical tools, such as Bregman domain functions and more general Kantorovich type problems. The connection between RMPR and flight control is expected to deepen as the design of autonomous systems becomes increasingly intertwined with performance, robustness, and safety requirements. This work establishes a comprehensive framework for compressive autoencoders through a theoretical lens, deriving key results and developing several employable techniques in tandem. A mathematical model is formulated to quantify the effectiveness of compressive autoencoders in dimensionality reduction, informed by principles from information theory. By treating the compressor and autoencoder as a unified system and optimizing its performance, we obtain specific designs for the compressor and encoder that minimize reconstruction error while meeting given compression ratios. Building upon this framework, we propose several practical methods for designing custom compressors and encoders in line with the obtained theoretical bounds. Moreover, we conduct numerical experiments to validate the accuracy and efficiency of our proposed techniques. Specifically, we apply the developed framework to analyze the characteristics of CNN layers as well-informed compressors and demonstrate the development of custom encoders for CIFAR10 and MNIST using the derived designs. Moreover, we successfully implemented the proposed techniques in a self-driving vehicle application, enabling the efficient compression of RGB images captured from the vehicle's camera without noticeable loss of performance. The source code for the experiments is publicly accessible at https://github.com/guoyong2016/CCA. Additionally, a binary connection-specific category is established, along with the representation theorem for first-order binary connection-valued theories. We examine the implications of this theory in continuous geometry. This commentary is based on a seminar held at Carnegie-Mellon University in 1999-2000. Although the original presentation included minor omissions, a few key aspects have been added to ensure clarity. A comprehensive list of relevant papers can be found at the end of this commentary. 

1. Introduction

First-order spectra with binary connections serve as a representation for categorical approaches to continuous geometry. This theory can be viewed as an extension of spectrum theory, and our analysis focuses on the key characteristics of first-order binary connection-valued theories. 

2. First-order spectra with binary connections

First-order binary connection-valued theories can be categorized into distinct types, and we concentrate on the binary connection with partial algebras. A first-order binary connection $\mathrel{R}$ in a theory $T$ satisfies certain conditions, including:
- For every formula $\phi(x,y)$, if $T$ does not prove $\exists y\phi(x,y)$, then $T$ does not prove $\forall x\phi(x,x)$.
- For every formula $\phi(x,y)$, if $T$ does not prove $\exists y\phi(x,y)$, then $T$ does not prove $\exists x\phi(x,y)$.
- For every formula $\phi(x,y)$, if $T$ proves $\exists y\phi(x,y)$, then $T$ proves $\exists y\mathrel{R}x,y$.
- For every formula $\phi(x,y)$, if $T$ proves $\exists y\phi(x,y)$, then $T$ proves $\exists x\mathrel{R}x,y$.

We established that the above conditions are unnecessary and can be replaced by two simplified constraints:
- If $\phi(x,y)$ is in $T$ and $x\neq y$, then $T$ proves $\exists y\mathrel{R}x,y$.
- If $\phi(x,y)$ is in $T$ and $x\neq y$, then $T$ proves $\exists x\mathrel{R}x,y$.

In the field of machine learning, especially in predictive modeling, it is essential to select the most relevant features from available data variables to improve model accuracy and efficiency.  Feature selection methods can be broadly categorized into three approaches: wrapper methods, filter methods, and hybrid approaches.  The latter two techniques are filter methods that are fastest in computation but may lack composable and efficient results compared to wrapper methods.  This study proposes a new hybrid approach called Hidden Space Mapping (HisMap) that leverages the strengths of both wrapper and filter methods to effectively tackle complex feature selection challenges in big data environments.  HisMap integrates the predictive power of supervised learning algorithms with the dimensionality reduction capabilities of unsupervised learning methods to efficiently map hidden data variables to observable ones.  To evaluate HisMap's performance, extensive experiments were conducted on 29 open-source datasets spanning various data sizes, types, and domains.  Notably, HisMap leaped above 90% of the benchmark methods in an unbiased comparison and outperformed the top 8 filter methods by a significant margin of 157.14% in feature selection accuracy.  Moreover, HisMap leaped above 97.14% of the benchmark methods in a comprehensive comparison with 21 other wrapper methods.  To validate HisMap's efficiency, experiments were conducted on 8 big data datasets, and the results showed that it outperformed 114 state-of-the-art filter methods by reducing feature selection computational complexity by at least an order of magnitude. Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled the creation of highly accurate classifiers, prompting researchers to explore novel attack methods that exploit specific flaws in how data is generated. Our research focuses on a unique type of attack where an adversary manipulates data in a targeted manner, specifically on financial data. We examined whether a sophisticated adversarial model could deceive a machine learning classifier by deliberately altering financial data, and found that such attacks are possible under specific conditions. Our analysis showed that the adversarial model can create artificial transactions, altering transaction IDs, amounts, and dates to compromise the classifier. To carry out the attack, the adversary must manipulate multiple data fields. We also found that changing transaction amounts is sufficient to fool the classifier, highlighting the vulnerability of machine learning models to targeted attacks exploiting specific flaws in data generation. Our study used a specific adversarial model and financial data, but its implications suggest that various types of data and adversarial models may be susceptible to similar attacks. Consequently, developers should prioritize protecting their models against targeted attacks exploiting specific data generation flaws. We also released an open-source advisory to facilitate research and sharing of adversarial models. Climate change denial is an ongoing issue on social media platforms, especially when it comes to established facts like temperature increases. Understanding conspiracy theories requires access to a comprehensive dataset, particularly one that identifies climate-related conspiracy theories and distinguishes established facts from false information. Our research focuses on the most prevalent climate conspiracy theories and how they spread on social media, as well as their connection to core themes and underlying beliefs. We also analyzed the impact of conspiracy theories on public perception of climate change, revealing a significant correlation despite our initial expectations. In fact, we found that social media users who engage with conspiracy theories are more likely to believe that climate change is not real, even if we control for other factors. To promote accurate climate discussions, we suggest implementing social media guidelines that explicitly address conspiracy theories. A related dataset is available at: https://climate-myths.org/en/dataset. Please note that this work is related to the project "Climate Myths": https://climate-myths.org. It is also part of a larger study on conspiracy theories in the context of climate change, wind energy, and infectious diseases, as described at: https://conspiracy-detection.com. This project aims to provide comprehensive datasets covering various domains of conspiracy theories, enabling researchers to explore the connection between conspiracy theories and climate change, as well as effective counter-measures. We hope this work will contribute to society by presenting fact-checking results in an accessible manner. It is expected that social media platforms will be crucial in disseminating accurate information to counter conspiracy theories, especially with the growing popularity of short-video platforms like TikTok. Therefore, we suggest collaborating with these companies to promote our research and present it in a way that is easily understandable by the general public. Additionally, we propose implementing a "climate change denier detection" tool on these platforms to alert users when they engage with posts promoting established conspiracy theories. We also suggest working with technology companies to make our research more accessible to the public, as well as providing alerts to social media users when they come across conspiracy theories related to climate change, wind energy, and infectious diseases. This could be achieved by using fact-checking results, as presented on our website (climate-myths.org), to present users with a summary of conspiracy theories, along with the related conspiracy theories and established facts. To further detail our ideas, please refer to our project description at: https://climate-myths.org. We believe that social media platforms can play a vital role in disseminating accurate climate information to counter conspiracy theories, as well as promoting established conspiracy theories

Studies of solar type II bursts via radio interferometry have revealed intricate patterns of moving sources. These sources, which emit radio waves at various frequencies, can be explained by a dynamic stellar flare scenario where a moving and dynamically changing magnetic field system causes the radio wave emission. This research utilizes radio interferometry to analyze a solar burst detected on ARK imager and MERTIS instruments on board Solar Orbiter, showing that the burst source linked to a stellar flare event exhibits an unexpected behavior. Observations indicate that the source characteristics demonstrate linked evolution, specifically, the source appears as a moving, point-like entity with increasing apparent speed and direction, and complex rotation. Notably, the source's apparent speed exceeds the speed of sound in the solar atmosphere, and its rotation covers an extensive frequency range. Additionally, the source exhibits an unusual, cone-shaped, moving pattern in space, and changes in its orientation in the frequency-cone plane over time. Analysis using a dynamic stellar flare model reveals the source characteristics can be effectively explained by a stellar flare entity experiencing a microflare, resulting in a changing magnetic field system consisting of a main loop and two smaller sub-loops. This research demonstrates that the source behavior can be effectively modeled using a dynamic stellar flare model with complex magnetic field systems, and provides new insights into the complex magnetic field system behavior during a microflare. Furthermore, the model confirms that a dynamic stellar flare entity can explain the observed source characteristics, and is consistent with observations of moving sources in solar bursts via radio interferometry. The research paves the way for future studies on the rapid changes in the complex magnetic field system supporting stellar flare entities. The code for the dynamic stellar flare model is available at https://github.com/andreimars/Code_SCAFF Fallen Tree/blob/main/dynamic_stellar_flare.py. Additionally, the ARK and MERTIS data utilized in this research can be accessed via the Solar Orbiter data hub at https://solarscorporation-ao.atlas.io/. The research has been thoroughly cited with relevant studies on stellar flare behavior via radio interferometry and dynamic modeling. In particular, the research references a study on dynamic stellar flare models and their consistency with radio interferometry data, as well as another study highlighting the complex magnetic field system characteristics in stellar flare entities. We investigate the existence of minimized solutions to the problem of finding ground states in the context of the biharmonic Choquard equation, where the exponent in the nonlinearity exceeds the critical value associated with the Laplacian, under the constraint of fixed $L^2$-norm in the field $u$, within the context of $H^2$-functions that decay at infinity in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The minimization problem is represented by the expression $\inf_{\|u\|_{L^2} = 1} I(u)$, where $I(u)$ corresponds to the energy functional evaluated at $u$, which includes a biharmonic term, a nonlocal interaction potential and an exponential nonlinearity. To resolve this problem, we utilize a standardization procedure that incorporates a Fourier multiplier with high frequency decay and constructized infrastructure such as the existence of standardizing functions, the $\hat{g}$-norm in the space of high frequency functions and a first order approximation of the $\hat{g}$-norm in space, all of which are detailed in the paper's supporting proofs. Following standardizing the problem, we demonstrate that nonradial minimized solutions exist in the space of high frequency functions with non-zero radial components. Moreover, we establish that the minimized solutions are necessarily radially symmetric and monotone in the distance from the origin when the nonlinearity's exponent is less than $\frac{9}{5}$. Finally, we show that the minimized solutions are elements of $C^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ when the nonlinearity's exponent is less than $\frac{9}{5}$. Additionally, we provide a method for explicitly calculating the minimized solutions when the nonlinearity's exponent is less than $\frac{9}{5}$. The main techniques employed in this study are the method of standardization, the method of high and low frequency decomposition and the use of a nonlocal variational structure in the analysis of the biharmonic Choquard equation. The study is significant as it is the first to investigate the existence of minimized solutions in the context of the biharmonic Choquard equation, particularly under the constraint of fixed $L^2$-norm in the field $u$, within the context of $H^2$-functions that decay at infinity in $\mathbb{R}^3$ where the exponent in the nonlinearity exceeds the critical value associated with the Laplacian. The extraction of identity information from text-based documents plays a crucial role in numerous applications across various domains. In Indonesia, where numerous official documents are scanned or digitally stored as images, a leading optical character recognition method is employed to obtain text data. However, the data captured in these texts is often incomplete, necessitating the application of natural language processing techniques to fill in the gaps. A key challenge arises from the incomplete or missing information in these documents, which requires the derivation of identity information from other data points. Despite the prevalence of identity information extraction tasks, there remains a significant shortage of publicly available datasets in Indonesia, limiting the development of effective and accurate models. Furthermore, a comparative analysis is conducted on different optical character recognition engines to determine the most effective method for extracting identity information. Additionally, the integration of natural language processing is found to enhance the overall accuracy of the proposed model. All related code and datasets are openly accessible on GitHub, enabling replication and future development on this unique Indonesian ID card extraction task. The models developed in this research hold promising potential for real-world applications, such as verifying customers' identity, validating users during online transactions, and granting access to restricted information, among others. With continued advancements, this technology can contribute positively to Indonesia's national development. The proposed approach is evaluated through simulations and the outcomes indicate that it outperforms conventional methods, offering enhanced accuracy and performance resilience in the face of channel impairments. This resourcefulness makes the proposed method an industry-friendly solution. The outcomes of this study demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over existing methods, solidifying its position as a reliable and accurate approach for 802.11p channel estimation. Recent breakthroughs in image classification have demonstrated the effectiveness of different architectures, such as Decision Trees, Linear Models, and Bi-RRT (Binary Reconfigurable Neural Tree), in achieving exceptional accuracy. However, their applications in computer vision are largely limited due to their rigid structures, lack of modularity, and inability to effectively utilize large amounts of data. In order to overcome these constraints and create models suitable for computer vision tasks, we introduce the Modulated Cyclic Activation (MCA) component, which enables the creation of complex, non-linear local functions. We utilize MCA in the Local Functional Graph, a novel neural network architecture, and evaluate its performance on a range of benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to produce highly accurate results. Specifically, it surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art Linear Models and Decision Trees on small datasets and rivals the performance of Bi-RRT on large datasets. Notably, it consistently produces results that are on par with or superior to those of pre-trained CNNs on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. Moreover, we find that the resulting models exhibit exceptional generalization capabilities, as demonstrated by their outstanding performance on the ImageNet dataset. Current AI systems face significant challenges when dealing with unpredictable deployments in real-world environments, characterized by unforeseen data discrepancies. In this study, we introduce a novel framework for adapting AI models to accommodate unexpected data changes during their operational lifespan. Our innovative approach leverages domain expertise to identify the underlying causes of these shifts and develops a strategy to mitigate their impact. We illustrate the effectiveness of this framework through a practical case study involving image classification, where we successfully modified an AI model to perform accurately in a hospital setting, despite being initially trained on images from the Internet and subsequently fine-tuned using cause-and-effect information and a limited dataset of high-quality, hospital-sourced images. Experimental results show that our semi-generative modeling approach produces better results compared to existing AI debiasing methods. Furthermore, we reflect on the broader implications of this research, highlighting its potential to bridge the gaps between AI model development, deployment, and fine-tuning in various applications. Our computational resources and related materials are freely accessible online. In recent years, deep learning methods have achieved remarkable success across a variety of domains. Despite their effectiveness, there is a noticeable lack of comprehensive geometric and analytical studies examining the underlying structures of these techniques. This paper seeks to explore the geometric and topological foundations of deep learning methods by examining popular examples such as neural networks with a single hidden layer, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks. By leveraging connectionist learning approaches and integrating concepts from Riemannian geometry and dynamical systems, we study the geometric properties of these structures and their associated algorithms. Specifically, we investigate the local and global convergence of these algorithms on specific datasets, and provide simplified analytical explanations for complex deep learning methods. Furthermore, we identify potential research avenues within the field of machine learning that can be addressed through geometric and topological analysis. Ultimately, this paper serves as a comprehensive introduction to the study of machine learning through geometric and topological lenses. Due to the extensive nature of this work, we have created a publicly accessible archive of supplementary materials that contain additional details. Additionally, the corresponding instructor's manual is available under a CC-BY license.

A new method, called Distorting CMB×LSS and examined through simulations with a focus on cross-correlations with galaxy surveys, is presented. This method involves evaluating how non-Gaussian distortions affect these correlations by comparing observed bispectra with mock ones created through cosmic simulation, which will be used to assess inflationary models. As a test, it is demonstrated that future DESI and LSST surveys will be sensitive to $k_{max}$ values of around 0.2-$0.3$ rad/m, which is slightly lower than the current limit set by the tomographic case. However, the limiting factor will not be the surveys themselves,  but rather the accuracy of the cosmic simulation, specifically the modeling of non-linear galaxy bias, which has the potential to impact future BIS findings.  As a result, it appears that future DESI and LSST surveys will be able to rule out models that have already been excluded through other observations and may be able to set limits on models that are consistent with the current understanding of the universe.  Therefore, it can be concluded that future cross-correlation surveys will have the ability to rule out models that have already been excluded through other observations and may be able to set limits on models that are consistent with the current understanding of the universe.  Ultimately, it appears that cosmic simulation accuracy will be the deciding factor in what models can be excluded through future BIS observations. We have developed a robust frequency estimation procedure that can withstand malicious interference from an adversary attempting to manipulate measurement data in wireless sensor networks. By assuming the adversary follows a known distribution and using a well-designed Bayesian estimator with Laplace weighting, we can limit estimation error while maintaining certain limits on the adversary's data manipulation, adhering to predetermined performance metrics such as maximum correlation distance and total variation distance. This robustness is achieved through the application of a Laplace concentration inequality. Furthermore, we have investigated the minimum amount of data required for reliable frequency estimation, deriving both upper and lower bounds using information theory. Specifically, we have explored the minimum amount of data required for estimating a binomial distribution and a uniform distribution on the integers 0 through k. This research provides insight into the minimum amount of data required for robust frequency estimation. Furthermore, we have investigated the minimum amount of data required for detecting whether a uniform distribution has been shifted by announcing the shift. This research has led to the identification of a tradeoff between robustness and sample complexity. We have demonstrated that estimators designed with certain constraints can be less effective than those that do not adhere to these constraints, even when robustness is prioritized. This research provides a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between robustness and sample complexity. We have also investigated the application of our procedures in a real-world scenario, using a wireless sensor network to estimate the frequency of a signal containing a step function. This research has shown that robust frequency estimation procedures can be effectively used in real-world settings. This research contributes to our knowledge of robust frequency estimation, enhancing our understanding of the field by providing new insights. Firstly, we have shown that robust frequency estimation can be accomplished within specified parameters using a Bayesian approach. Secondly, we have identified sample size requirements for reliably estimating a uniform distribution on the integers 0 through k. Specifically, we have found that taking the fewest samples equal to k plus one is sufficient for reliably estimating a uniform distribution. Furthermore, we have explored the application of our procedures in real-world settings, using a wireless sensor network to estimate the frequency of a signal containing a step function. This research has shown the practical value of our procedures in real-world settings. This research further contributes to our knowledge of robust frequency estimation by answering previously unaddressed questions. In early 2020, China experienced an unprecedented COVID-19 epidemic that sparked a widespread spread of digital rumors through social media platforms. These rumors not only caused public anxiety but also led to the mobilization of fact-checking groups. In an effort to contain the spread of misinformation, the Chinese government launched an official campaign to disseminate accurate information to counter the rumors. This study investigates the propagation patterns of digital rumors in China by analyzing data from Weibo, a prominent micro-blogging platform, and examines the impact of official fact-checking efforts as well as the role of social media users in disseminating rumorous content. The results show that digital rumors were primarily spread through social media, particularly during the early stages of the epidemic, and that the government's fact-checking efforts were effective in halting their dissemination. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that certain social media users, such as celebrities and media outlets, played a significant role in amplifying digital rumors, resulting in wider circulation. The research provides valuable insights for researchers working on misinformation spread in non-Western contexts and offers practical recommendations for combating digital rumors in China. Additionally, the study's findings are relevant to researchers exploring the role of fact-checking in diverse social media ecosystems. The analyzed data is available on GitHub, including the complete research paper, data dictionaries, and dissemination materials. The associated Weibo project is also accessible online. The research builds on previous studies on misinformation spread in China, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, and contributes to the body of work examining the role of social media in global health crises. The study was enabled by a collaborative research grant from the Science Foundation for Leveraging Social Media, which supported a project involving fact-checking groups, academia, and industry stakeholders. The grant allowed for the employment of two research assistants who collected and annotated data under the guidance of leading academics. The project's aims were aligned with the grant's objectives, which focused on understanding misinformation spread in China through social media. The study's results are consistent with the grant's goals, which encompassed combating digital rumors, analyzing misinformation patterns, and exploring the role of fact-checking. The funded project also resulted in two additional studies examining the dissemination of digital rumors in China, particularly in the context of COVID-19. The first study investigated the propagation of rumors related to conspiracy theories, while the second study focused on the role of social media users in disseminating rumorous content. The associated data is available on GitHub, including the complete research papers, data dictionaries, and dissemination materials.

The increasing accessibility to hyperspectral imaging data has facilitated a variety of applications, yet the vast dimensionality of this data creates significant difficulties for subsequent analysis and interpretation. Numerous techniques have been developed to reduce this data's complexity, applying methods such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Our research investigates the effects of utilizing PCA on hyperspectral pixel classification tasks, applying three different dimensionsality reduction approaches in comparison to a baseline that utilizes the original hyperspectral data. The analysis reveals that PCA's impacts are highly scene-dependent and can either harm or improve classification performance. Consequently, we suggest that dimensionality reduction should not be undertaken hastilly in hyperspectral applications, and instead, such reductions should be carried out with caution and careful consideration. The methodology employed in this study is made accessible through our public repository, enabling other researchers to reproduce our results and apply our approach to various other datasets. The repository can be found at: https://github.com/50thLink/HPC_Cyclone-Classification.git. The dataset utilized in this research, consisting of hyperspectral images captured over agricultural areas in Chile, is owned by Dr. Christian R. Romero of the University of Santiago of Chile's Valpara\u00fdo Metropolitan University. The dataset's specifications include 211 bands, 800x800 pixels, and 5 classes, featuring diverse spatial and temporal complexity. The data was captured using the hyperspectral camera 'HISOP-150', which is equipped with 190 spectral bands, capturing the spectral range from 400 to 900 nm. The spectral resolution enables the differentiation between various biological species' characteristics. The data's accessibility is restricted due to ongoing data collection by Dr. Christian R. Several prominent NLP frameworks share a common goal: to translate natural language into a format that can be processed by machines. While they achieve this goal in different ways, their approaches often result in distinct representation languages. In this paper, we explore the possibility of reducing these frameworks to a single, fundamental formalism. Specifically, we demonstrate that Type Theory with Millikanski types can simulate the representations of at least four notable NLP frameworks: Sequent Calculus, Natural Deduction, and two variants of Gamma. By establishing this reduction, we gain two important benefits. Firstly, we clarify the underlying assumptions of NLP frameworks regarding natural language meaning. Secondly, we open the door for using powerful logical tools to analyze NLP frameworks. Furthermore, this reduction enables us to investigate whether a given NLP framework can accurately capture the semantics of natural language, effectively serving as a benchmark for evaluating the design of NLP frameworks. Ultimately, this line of inquiry holds potential for significant contributions to the fields of both programming languages and natural language processing. Additionally, this reduction has given rise to novel applications of logical concepts, such as domain-theoretic semantics, differential categories, and substructural logics, to NLP domains. Specifically, we show how to interpret Gamma's domain theory and its partial order in the context of natural language. Furthermore, we propose a system of differential types for modelling the dynamics of natural language. Lastly, we investigate how the substructural logic of exponentiation can be employed in modelling the scope of reference in natural language. In particular, we explore how the absence of contraction modality can be used to model the scope of reference in natural language and how the absence of the exchange modality can be used to model the order of sentences. Moreover, we propose a system of exchange-free differential types for modelling the dynamics of natural language. In particular, we study a sentence tokenisation problem using the concept of differential categories. In this regard, we explore the exchange-free modelling of sentence tokenisation as a process of multiplication in a category and show that the absence of exchange does not hinder it. In particular, we demonstrate that sentence tokenisation can be modelled by a pair of monoidal products in a category of differential types and that the absence of contraction is sufficient for this modelling to operate effectively. Residual random errors in molecular dynamics simulations can hinder the accuracy of analysis, particularly when examining subtle correlations between certain distances. We developed a protocol to validate and refine the structures of proteins using simulated average positions of amide proton chemical shifts. This protocol utilizes quantum-mechanical calculations to determine how protein structures affect the chemical shifts of their amide protons, enabling the distinction between correct and incorrect protein conformations. We tested this protocol by applying it to a 100-ns simulation of ubiquitin, which revealed a high correlation between predicted chemical shifts and actual experimental data. We also demonstrated the ability to refine protein structures using this protocol, resulting in improved agreement between simulated and actual experimental data. This protocol could become a valuable tool for assessing the accuracy of protein structures and guiding their refinement in models used in protein design and development. However, we encountered some challenges in our research, such as the substantial computational requirements of quantum-mechanical calculations for large proteins. We propose utilizing machine learning methods to develop more efficient protocols that can be applied to longer proteins in the future. Ultimately, the development of more accurate and transferable residue-level relationships between protein structures and their effects on NMR shifts, such as chemical shifts, order parameters, and amide proton shifts, will be crucial for the successful application of this protocol to longer proteins, such as tubulins. We hope our research will contribute to this effort by providing previously unavailable quantum-mechanical data. We also believe that similar protocols for assessing the accuracy of other biomolecular structures will be developed in the future, such as mortrin, monomer, and models used in drug design. We envision these protocols will encourage further research in areas such as protein design, where researchers can utilize simulated structures to identify ideal protein conformations. We have opened access to our code and research data, inviting others to contribute to this project and develop more efficient protocols. We predict future developments will lead to the widespread use of simulated structures in fields such as protein design and research into how proteins treat diseases. We propose these protocols will enable researchers to simulate how proteins move and interact with other molecules. Recent research has shown that altering the loss function in deep learning can produce diverse results. This study aimed to explore the impact of changing loss functions in deep learning, specifically in classification tasks, and identify consistent outcomes. Unlike previous studies, our investigation focused on the practical effects of loss function variations rather than their theoretical underpinnings. We examined the practical implications of loss function choices through three key aspects: network architecture design, training methods, and data usage. Our analysis revealed that swapping loss functions typically leads to unpredictable outcomes in these areas. However, after thoroughly examining the literature, we identified one consistent effect of loss function alteration: it affects the stoppage of training. This study provides the first comprehensive assessment of the practical influence of loss function choices in deep learning. It also highlights potential applications of loss function manipulation, such as enhancing model robustness and data efficiency, and reducing the reliance on hyperparameter tuning. Furthermore, our investigation sheds light on the underlying causes of these effects, unlocking new research directions. Ultimately, this study seeks to stimulate discussions on the influence of loss functions and their practical implications in deep learning. With further research, we hope to deepen our understanding of these connections. The proposed approach can be found at https://github.com/bczhangb/loss-impact. Additionally, our accompanying video can be viewed at https://youtu.be/6h6k0T4c0Oc. Starting with a set of single-particle orbitals and their corresponding energies,
the parquet theory constructs a theoretical framework for describing complex many-body
interactions by breaking them down into a series of lower-dimensional geometric
decompositions, each corresponding to a specific type of interaction, such as
nearest-neighbor interactions for a lattice system. By applying a graphical representation,
parquet theory can analyze the effects of multiple-body interactions and ensure the
consistency of resulting approximations. In our study, we demonstrate that parquet
theory can be represented as a self-consistent many-body theory derived from a Hamiltonian
model, in which interactions are encapsulated in a Hamiltonian and the parquet
approximations arise from a natural geometric decomposition, in the case of a
nearest-neighbor-hopping lattice and a Hubbard model. Furthermore, we show that
this view of parquet theory allows for a direct application to the study of
interacting fermions, in particular to the study of a Hubbard model where we find
that within the framework of a self-consistent many-body theory, we can derive
results consistent with known results including the Mott transition and
Luttinger-theory behavior at the Fermi point. This new perspective on parquet
theory offers a promising approach to the study of interacting fermions and other
many-body systems, and may provide valuable insights into their behavior.

In the US, law enforcement uses various systems to process and analyze incident reports, but the wealth of information within these reports often remains underutilized. Each report offers a firsthand glimpse into the individuals involved, their interactions with dispatchers, and the incidents themselves. Effective communication between users and dispatchers is crucial, and their interactions hold significant value for understanding how incidents unfold and how people respond to emergency situations. By incorporating machine learning-based techniques, the hidden insights embedded in these conversations can be uncovered, yielding constructive insights for enhancing user-dispatcher interactions. Through a comprehensive analysis of over 180,000 incident calls, our research revealed crucial findings, including the most frequently used words, phrases, canbacks, and emotions expressed across various emergency situations. Moreover, our investigation demonstrated how effectively human dispatchers adapt to changing situations and utilize contextual information to differentiate between similar incidents. Ultimately, our research not only provides valuable knowledge but also serves as a foundation for developing intelligent systems that facilitate more informed and effective communications between users and dispatchers. Our research adheres to the highest ethical standards, as outlined in the corresponding moral-ethical guidelines. Moreover, our study respects individuals' right to privacy by removing all personally identifiable information from the incident calls before analysis. Lastly, our research strives to maintain transparency by clearly illustrating our methods and showcasing the obtained results. When a part of a compound called a superconductor exposes itself to a powerful magnetic field, its ability to conduct electricity without resistance changes. This happens because the magnetic field affects the Cooper pairs, which are pairs of electrons that give rise to the phenomenon of superconductivity, and in this particular case, breaks them apart into individual components. Although the broken pairs can move freely again, they no longer function as a single entity, thus contributing to the paramagnetic response, which in this context, is a hallmark of the triplet nature of the Cooper pairs. This process can be observed in the superconductor Cs$_{2}$CoCl$_{4}$(H$_{2}$O)$_{2}$$\cdot$2D$_{2}$O by adjusting the magnetic field's strength and temperature, and in this study, we simulate this phenomenon and confirm that the observed effects are consistent with the triplet nature of the Cooper pairs. This triad nature is in line with earlier research, which suggested that the Cooper pairs in this compound consist of three coordinated quantum entities, and this triad nature is in line with the phenomenon of nematic superconductivity, which is a type of exotic superconducting behavior characterized by the triad's directional properties.
