Convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks. However, their use in classifying climate types from aerial images is a complex task due to the diversity of possible weather conditions (64 classes in the newly created Climate dataset). Traditional evaluation methods are often inadequate, using only accuracy as a metric to gauge a model's performance. To address this limitation, we developed the Climate dataset, consisting of 64 climate types, and adapted the ICM2019 dataset to complement it. We then evaluated several convolutional neural network architectures on these datasets to establish a benchmark for future comparisons. Our analysis explores the effectiveness of pre-trained models, data augmentation, and inverse data augmentation on the two datasets. Notably, we discovered that utilizing pre-trained models can lead to overfitting in the Climate dataset, and that inverse data augmentation may negatively impact a model's accuracy when applied to both the Climate and ICM2019 datasets. Our work is further exemplified by the development of a system that utilizes aerial images to determine the prevailing weather conditions, demonstrating an accuracy of 51.64% without prior knowledge of the weather and 68.45% with prior knowledge of the weather on the Climate dataset. Our research is publicly accessible through GitHub, including the Climate dataset, codes, and model implementations for easy reproduction and comparison. The Climate dataset can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/cdebuine/Climate-classes. The ICM2019 dataset can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/epfl-sigproc-summer-school/ICM2019. The Climate dataset consists of 64 climate types, and we adapted the ICM2019 dataset to complement it by selecting images that align with these climate types. The accuracy of a model is assessed by calculating the numerical closeness of the predicted class to the actual class. The class with the highest predicted probability is considered the model's prediction. Notwithstanding the complexity of classifying climate types, we found that inverse data augmentation can negatively impact a model's accuracy, and that pre-trained models can lead to overfitting in the Climate dataset. Our analysis is based on evaluating several convolutional neural network architectures on two datasets, the Climate dataset with 64 climate types and the ICM2019 dataset, utilizing aerial images classified into 39 climate types. The understanding of climate change among various segments of society is influenced by distinct information sources, such as media, scientific findings and economic implications. To explore the dynamics of societal perspectives on climate change, we examined how different groups incorporate new information into their worldviews. A longitudinal study of public opinion surveys in the US revealed that discussions of climate change in politics and the media's coverage are reflected in shifting societal views. In contrast, the views of business and industry leaders tend to lag behind the public's perceptions, and even when presented with evidence of the economic impacts of climate change, their perspectives do not significantly alter. Our findings indicate a need for a more in-depth, real-time understanding of the interactions among societal views of climate change and the roles played by diverse groups and information sources. We also suggest that policy makers should consider the societal perspectives on climate change that are influenced by the perspectives of the general public, rather than solely relying on the views of business and industry leaders. Finally, we propose that climate change education in academic and professional settings should be improved by making the discussions of climate change more relevant and meaningful to the perspectives of the audience. We also suggest the use of public engagement strategies that are grounded in a social movement approach to enhance the discussions of climate change and reduce the differences between the perspectives of the audience and the experts. We propose a novel virtual model for controlling the movement of soft grippers using a simplified representation of their deformation. This model, integrated with the Koopman operator theory for dimensionality reduction, enables efficient representation of the virtual model's dynamics. We have developed a corresponding controller strategy that utilizes the simplified structure and make corresponding adjustments to optimize performance. The integrated virtual model and controller system allows for rapid and efficient training of parameter settings. The approach has been successfully validated through simulation and experimental comparison with prior art on a specific soft gripper design. Additionally, we have demonstrated its applicability to a three-finger soft gripper design with multiple fingers. Further development of this methodology could enable seamless digital twin creation and inform the design of advanced soft robotics technologies. Advanced high-resolution spectrometers enable the reconstruction of a broad spectrum of baryonic energy density as light travels through the intergalactic medium. Nevertheless, the current limitation of high-resolution spectrometers restricts such studies to the redshift range of 0 to 3.5. A neural network model has been developed to bypass this constraint, allowing the reconstruction of the energy density spectrum at higher baryonic densities beyond a redshift of 3.5 using a relatively small dataset of 18 cosmological spectra collected from quasars at redshifts greater than 3. 

This neural network was trained using a dataset from the Baryon Oscillation Spectrum Survey (BOSS) DR12 and verified with additional data from higher-resolution spectrometers, demonstrating good agreement between the reconstructed and original data. Notably, the reconstruction accurately differentiates between various matter density models, including $\Lambda$CDM, WCDM, and SCADM, with uncertainties decreasing with data quality. The method's potential to analyze large datasets from future surveys, such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), is significant, enabling the detection of changing cosmological parameters and the evolution of baryonic energy density with high precision. 

This detection could result in modified structure formation models or new physics beyond $\Lambda$CDM, requiring validation from structure formation simulations to confirm the findings. Furthermore, the analysis of future datasets from DESI may enable the detection of changing cosmological parameters and baryonic energy density with high precision, leading to a better understanding of the universe's evolution. 

The code for reconstructing the energy density spectrum has been made publicly available on GitHub. Although initially trained using a relatively small dataset, the neural network model has demonstrated promising accuracy and scalability, suggesting the method's potential to greatly expand our knowledge of the universe's baryonic energy density with the analysis of future large-scale surveys.

Another study has demonstrated the development of a neural network model to predict the signal of baryonic oscillations within the spectra of quasars at high redshift, using a small dataset collected from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS).

various NBA teams. The code for this project is available on GitHub for public access.

A key objective in artificial intelligence is to derive causal inferences from limited observational data and unstable interventions. Current methods use symbolic or numerical representations to model this process, although the interplay between these methods remains poorly understood in this context. To address this knowledge gap, we developed the Signaling Game framework, a multi-agent interaction that combines symbolic and analog interactions to study emergent semantic exchanges between agents. We demonstrated that analog interactions alone can lead to accurate inferences without requiring explicit models of the underlying causal structures. Furthermore, we showed that merging analog and symbolic data results in more efficient inference outcomes than using analog data in isolation. These findings have broad applications in artificial intelligence, as they underscore the potential for emergent representations to yield beneficial outcomes. To facilitate further research, we released the Signaling Game framework as an open-source Python package at https://github.com/dschnidr/signaling-game for community use. Signaling Game is currently compatible with PyTorch 1.10 and 1.11, but we plan to support later versions in future updates. Moreover, we created a companion website at https://dschnidr.github.io/signaling-game that provides a interactive demo and a comprehensive guide to the Signaling Game framework. Future updates will also include the addition of more environments, such as multi-agent scenarios, as well as a comprehensive empirical evaluation of the framework. Ultimately, we aim for the Signaling Game framework to serve as a general-purpose tool for tackling challenging artificial intelligence problems. Recent advances in session-based suggestion systems have led to the development of a new category of intelligent interfaces that utilize session-based data to offer relevant information to users. These systems work by capturing a user's browsing behavior within a session and providing personalized content suggestions throughout the user's search process. However, standard session-based suggestion systems fail to account for the inherent duality present in many users' search behaviors, which can manifest as simultaneous interests in multiple categories of content. To address this limitation, we develop a two-phase recommender system that uses a rank representation learning method to suggest relevant items to users while considering their current session-driven interests. Furthermore, we integrate this method into a narrative summarization framework to facilitate the communication of a user's complex multi-faceted search intentions to suggested content through narrative summaries. Experiment results demonstrate that our two-phase recommender system surpasses current benchmarks in recommendation performance and outperforms other enhanced systems that incorporate narrative summaries in user engagement metrics. To facilitate reproduction of our results, we will make our implemented code available on GitHub. Additionally, we will make our dataset of rank representation learning objectives and narrative summarization datasets available under the terms of the MIT license. This dataset can be utilized by the broader AI research community as a resource for developing new methods in the areas of session-based suggestion systems and narrative summarization. Moreover, we will make our developed website (ranksum.com) publicly accessible, where users can interact with our two-phase recommender system through narrative summarization. This will enable users to engage with our system on a larger scale and allow us to collect and analyze additional user feedback in the future. Ultimately, we aim for our developed system to enhance the overall user experience in session-based suggestion systems while maintaining high levels of relevance in suggested content. To achieve this goal, we will continually monitor user feedback and make necessary adjustments to our method in the future. This research will significantly contribute to the advancement of AI research in the areas of session-based suggestion systems and narrative summarization by showcasing novel and effective solutions to established problems. This includes introducing a new two-phase recommender system with a narrative summarization framework that surpasses current benchmarks in relevance and user engagement. Moreover, we will make our developed system publicly accessible, enabling users to interact with our two-phase recommender system through narrative summarization under the terms of the MIT license. This will enable us to analyze user behavior and maintain relevance in suggested content while facilitating two-way communication between users and suggested content through narrative summaries. This research will demonstrate novel and effective solutions to established problems in AI

Consequently, even seemingly uniform stress levels in the active fluid give rise to flow around stationary particles and flow alignment with moving particles, as predicted by our analytical models and confirmed through numerical simulations. Sequence graphs, a type of bipartite graph derived from DNA or similar sequences, have an associated Seidel matrix whose eigenvalues and entry patterns hold significant analytical value. By examining the diagonal entries and off-diagonal nonzeros of the Seidel matrix, researchers gain insight into its eigenvalue spectrum, linking this information to possible Seidel matrix eigenvalue pairs, and ultimately, characterizing the range of these eigenvalues. Additionally, partial results concerning the characteristic polynomial of the Seidel matrix help estimate its eigenvalues, while the general approach can be applied to polyharmonic graphs, including sequence graphs, leading to an estimation of the eigenvalues' location and range. Interestingly, for DNA sequence graphs, the estimated upper limit of the Seidel matrix eigenvalues aligns closely with the DNA similarity measure's limit. Finally, the research estimates the total degree of the Seidel matrix, a measure of matrix energy, for DNA sequence graphs of varying lengths. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of DNA sequence graphs' topological structure and the sequence measure's relationship to the graph's combinatorial nature. Moreover, the research sheds light on the link between the sequence measure and the Seidel matrix's range, eigenvalue pairs, and eigenvalue spectrum. Ultimately, the study uncovers correlations and similarities between the sequence measure and the Seidel matrix, particularly in DNA graphs, but also extends to general polyharmonic graphs. These correlations raise intriguing hypotheses that the sequence measure and the Seidel matrix are interconnected, sharing common characteristics and properties. Furthermore, the research presents methods and tools to analyze the sequence measure and the Seidel matrix eigenvalue pairs, posing new questions and areas for further investigation in graph theory and bipartite graph analysis. These studies may lead to novel insights in molecular biology, DNA analysis, and similar fields, revealing underlying connections between the underlying graphs and the matrices that model these graphs. Additionally, the research may yield new perspectives on the eigenvalue pairs, range, and eigenvalue spectrum in matrix theory and linear algebra. Ultimately, the studies can be extended to general polyharmonic graphs, opening up new avenues for research and analysis. Furthermore, the papers present analogous research in the context of RNA graphs, exploring the underlying connections between the Frouhijeh-Rasmussen matrix, the sequence measure, and the graph's combinatorial nature. These connections raise important research questions and areas for further investigation in graph theory and bipartite graph analysis, as well as in molecular biology, DNA analysis, and similar fields. We are studying a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator with a periodic potential and finite-band properties on a two-dimensional torus. The finite-band property is represented by a band diagram that displays a well-resolved band when the potential is minimal. The operator's spectrum is analyzed using elliptic estimates, and it is shown that its spectrum lies within a finite-band structure as well. This research builds upon earlier work involving periodic Schrödinger operators with band gaps. Unlike those studies, we are able to provide accurate upper limits for eigenvalue eigenfunction pairs and explain their localization using minimal surfaces and a form of the Logvinenko-Sinai theorem. One interesting outcome is that we can confirm a conjecture initially proposed by Breuer and Herbst. Moreover, we are exploring connections between band structures and their associated graph topology. The non-self-adjoint nature of our operator leads to a broader definition of graph topology, incorporating concepts from spectral theory, dynamical systems, and quantum chaos. This research is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum chaos in two-dimensional systems. The band structure of our Dirac operator exhibits distinct features, such as non-trivial symmetries, zero-energy modes, and chiral symmetry, which are not observed in two-dimensional Schrödinger operators. These additional properties are rooted in the operator's matrix form and its relation to the Laplacian on a Riemannian surface with boundary. Specifically, we are examining surfaces with boundaries and exploring the consequences of chiral symmetry on band structures, zero-energy modes, and elliptic finite-band energies, particularly in relation to minimal band structures and elliptic finite-band energies. These research outcomes can be further generalized to study band structures in other Dirac operators, such as those defined on graph boundaries of 3D manifolds and bi-layers of 2D manifolds. The generalization of our research is facilitated by the broad applicability of elliptic estimates and spectral theory. The outcomes of our research are expected to contribute to the development of quantum systems with designed band structures, an essential feature in quantum chaos for studying exotic phenomena. Additionally, we are examining the transport properties of quantum systems with designed band structures, an area with significant technological applications and future potential for development. The research outcomes can be further utilized in the development of photonic devices with designed band structures. The extensive collection of Wikipedia articles provides a wealth of detailed data that can shed light on the activities of contributors. This data can be analyzed to identify automatic indicators of article quality, which is a significant challenge in current research. This paper contributes to the quest of automatically identifying low-quality articles on Wikipedia by examining patterns in editing behavior, including the frequency and content of modifications made by different groups of editors. Unlike previous studies that focus on assessing content quality, this research delves into the activities of Wikipedia editors to develop a predictive model of article quality, which yields a substantial accuracy rate of 90.5% using decision tree and random forest algorithms with pre-labeled articles, and 82.5% using predictive modeling with unlabelled articles, including unsupervised learning techniques such as decision tree classification and random forest classification. The accuracy of classification is significantly enhanced when incorporating features related to article discussions, including the presence, content, and modifications made to talk pages associated with each article. The patterns in editing behavior provide valuable insights into the quality of articles, and can be utilized to develop predictive models of article quality, including those based on contributions, edits, and discussions, as well as predictive modeling with Wikipedia pages using natural language features. The predictive model of article quality identifies not only individual articles but also articles within specific categories as high or low quality, and can be applied to various categories with minimal adjustments. The categories that were tested, including categories of high and low quality articles, were chosen because they contain articles that are representative of either category. The research demonstrates that analyzing patterns in editing behavior can provide a quantitative measure of article quality, which is often subject to qualitative assessments. The study also highlights the significance of considering the activities of various groups of editors when evaluating article quality, rather than just focusing on contributions or edits. We propose an innovative approach to transfer knowledge for classification tasks without additional training, by leveraging a pre-existing decision-boundary based black-box model. Our method enables seamless knowledge transfer for both single-source and multi-source scenarios with minimal modifications to the existing black-box model framework. Furthermore, we develop a metric to gauge the confidence level of the black-box model's decisions and demonstrate its practical utility in determining the knowledge transfer outcome. Our proposed technique is dissected and analyzed through comprehensive case studies. Specifically, we successfully applied it to transfer knowledge for both binary and multi-class classification tasks across diverse domains, which also included a synthetic dataset and a real-world clinical dataset. Our study shows that the black-box model's accuracy can be significantly improved through knowledge transfer, with up to a 35.61% increase in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we observed that the black-box model's performance after knowledge transfer can rival that of sophisticated machine learning models, such as Support Vector Machines and Random Forest. Our approach offers numerous benefits, including simplified model integration, streamlined knowledge acquisition, and enhanced decision-making confidence assessment. Ultimately, we believe that this knowledge transfer framework will facilitate the development of more sophisticated black-box model applications in various challenging and complex decision-making scenarios. The associated code can be accessed via the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ahmed-Ali-Zain/Decision-Based-Knowledge-Transfer. The employed black-box model framework can be obtained via the following link: https://github.com/IBM/DecisionService. The clinical dataset utilized in our study can be obtained via the following link: https://clinicalinformaticsresearch.github.io/clinical-institutions/. A detailed report on our findings is also available: https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2205.03091. Ahmed A. M. A study of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decays is conducted based on event data from the LHCb experiment, corresponding to either 3.0 or 6.0 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity. The observed ratio of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ to $\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decays is determined to be 0.127±0.017 (stat.) ± 0.016 (syst.), providing evidence for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ with significance exceeding 5 standard deviations. The branching fraction ratio of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ to $B^0_s\to J/\psi K^0_S$ is measured and found to be in agreement with predictions based on NLO perturbative QCD calculations. The observed branching fraction ratio is also compared to a model-based expectation of 0.133±0.006, revealing substantial discrepancies. The data are further used to set an upper limit on the ratio of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(-+)}\ell^+\ell^-$ to $B^0_s\to J/\psi\rho$ branching fractions, ranging from 0.7 to 3.8 times 10^-4, subject to certain conditions. The data are also utilized in investigating $\bar{B}^0_s$ decays to $\bar{D}^{(\ast)}$ mesons, decaying into various kaon-eta pairs, with the data used in constraining an effective four-quark interaction model describing $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0$ transitions. The data are also used in establishing upper limits on the ratio of $\bar{B}^0_s$ to $\bar{B}^0$ decays to $\bar{D}^{(\ast)}$ mesons in association with a neutral kaon. The data are further used in exploring $\bar{B}^0_s$ decays to $\bar{D}^{(\ast)}$ mesons in combination with a dijet system, with the data used in examining differential cross-section and forward-backward asymmetry patterns. Recent breakthroughs in human-robot collaboration using learning from human demonstration have greatly improved the efficiency of robot training. Nonetheless, this method has limitations when faced with tasks involving human-scale observation, where robots need to utilize information from multiple viewpoints to accomplish a goal. The current paradigm faces challenges in adapting human demonstrations to these complex observational environments, necessitating extensive expertise. To address this issue, we introduce a novel Co-Observation without Specialist Demonstration approach, combining data-driven and reinforcement learning techniques to enable robots to navigate and observe their surroundings, interact with objects, and make decisions through trial and error, ultimately achieving successful outcomes in simulated bin-picking scenarios. The results demonstrate that our proposed method enables robots to successfully complete observed tasks in uncharted environments, surpassing the performance of a baseline model that solely utilizes human demonstrations. The significant advancement of our Co-Observation without Specialist Demonstration approach opens up new avenues for collaborative robots to learn from experience, even in intricate observational environments characterized by multiple perspectives and complex decision-making requirements. Moreover, this work presents a fresh perspective on human-robot collaboration, emphasizing the potential for robots to autonomously acquire essential observation information, interact with objects, and make informed decisions, thereby reducing the dependence on specialist demonstrations. The novel paradigm has far-reaching implications for the development of collaborative robots, enabling them to effectively navigate and observe their surroundings, learn through trial and error, and achieve successful outcomes in a range of observed tasks. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted thorough experiments in simulated bin-picking scenarios, where the robot was required to navigate and observe its surroundings, interact with objects, and achieve successful outcomes. The results of these experiments clearly demonstrate that our Co-Observation without Specialist Demonstration approach enables robots to successfully complete observed tasks in uncharted environments, achieving a completion rate of 70% across 10 diverse bins. In contrast, the baseline model that solely utilized human demonstrations achieved a dismal completion rate of 20% for the same tasks. The substantial advancement of our Co-Observation without Specialist Demonstration approach offers a fresh perspective on human-robot collaboration, emphasizing the potential for robots to effectively navigate and observe their surroundings, learn through trial and error, and achieve successful outcomes, as evidenced by the significant improvement in completion rates. To further evaluate the efficacy of our Co-Observation without Specialist Demonstration approach, we conducted ablation experiments in simulated bin-picking scenarios, where the results demonstrated that our method outperformed a baseline model that solely utilized human demonstrations, achieving a 35% points higher completion

Multispectral data is used to measure and track the physical interactions between a person's hands and objects. This paper presents a novel approach called HOE that detects and tracks hand-object engagements in point cloud series, which are commonly captured in the real world. In contrast to traditional computer vision methods that rely on RGB information, HOE leverages depth and infrared data to ignore background noise and focus only on the interacting hands and objects. This is then combined with computer vision techniques that utilize spatial relationships, kinematic constraints, and appearance features to model hands and objects in 3D. As a result, HOE can accurately ignore weak interactions and focus only on the primary interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by using a combination of learning-based and knowledge-driven methods to evaluate its performance on various real-world datasets, which shows that HOE surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches by a significant margin. This paper then uses a multiple instance learning approach to leverage performance insights from multiple hands and objects in the same scene. Finally, we showcase the applications of HOE in video rebilding and engagement tracking. Our source code and datasets are available for public use. Our study also investigates the underlying crystallographic structure, demonstrating the existence of a 2-fold symmetry in the lattice. In addition, we have identified a collection of 10 distinct paths in this lattice, which exhibit a 2-fold symmetry interleave. This collection meets the criteria of a rank 4, 2-interleave 'tail-triangle' C-collection, thereby expanding the existing concept of star-triangle equivalence in the lattice. Furthermore, we have applied our results to analyze a lattice-based Markov chain, proving that the transition graph of this chain is 2-colorable. Our proof relies on the exploration of a collection of paths, termed 'colorful' paths, which exhibit a 2-fold symmetry interleave, meeting specific color matching criteria. These colorful paths are shown to be a subset of the above-mentioned C-collection. In a broader context, our work in this area is publicly accessible through interactive 3D visualizations on the https://lattice-paths.webcindinfo.com/ website. This online resource provides visualizations of the lattice, showcasing the associated Markov chain transition graph, as well as highlighting 'colorful' paths under different 2-coloring schemes. To assess the impact of treatment disruption on patient outcomes, we develop a novel framework for identifying treatment disruption periods based on patient similarity. This approach uses a proximity measure to determine areas on the outcome scale associated with treatment status, and subsequently marks periods of significant change in these areas as treatment disruption periods. Building on the work of Cox and O'Keefe, we expand upon their method for the K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN) interference framework by incorporating the dependence of patient outcomes on neighboring treatment status. We derive a test statistic to evaluate treatment disruption periods in the KNN framework and propose a semi-parametric procedure for point and interval estimation. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of this estimator under both small and large sample scenarios and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation studies. The utility of our method is showcased through its application to data from the National Longitudinal Study of Youth, where we identify distinct periods of treatment disruption among youth born to smoking mothers. Specifically, we find that there are notable transitions in the outcomes associated with smoking status among youth born to smoking mothers, particularly around the ages of 14 and 17, as observed in a figure included within the article. These results provide empirical support for prior research on the CDC's Guideline for Perinatal Care, where smoking cessation recommendations are outlined. We anticipate that our method will contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for various fields, where treatment disruption periods may hold significant practical value. Related code can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/AManohar9/TreatmentDisruption-KNNFramework. Please note that this research was previously presented at the 2022 INFORMS meeting in a paper titled "Identifying Treatment Disruption under the K-Nearest-Neighbors Interference Framework" and has since been published in the journal Biometrics in 2023. For the first time, our approach includes all possible Dark Matter annihilation channels, such as $\chi\chi\rightarrow \bar{e}e$, $\bar{\mu}\mu$, etc., in addition to neutrino-only channels like $\chi\chi\rightarrow \nu\bar{\nu}$. By employing a novel equilibrium condition, we have developed a streamlined method for deriving emissivity equations, facilitating the direct computation of neutrino emissions within the Dense Matter environment. Notably, our refined calculations reveal that neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations can be suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to the generally accepted estimate of Jutte and Mezzano, thereby opening the door for more stringent empirical constraints on the cross-section of Dark Matter interactions with nucleons. Furthermore, our study indicates that within the framework of Fermi Liquid Theory, neutrino emissions from quarks and gluons are negligible in comparison to the emissions from nucleons. Interestingly, our work also includes a detailed analysis of the emissivities resulting from the interaction of Dark Matter with nuclear cores, as well as with electrons and muons. Moreover, we have explored the implications of strong interaction many-body effects on neutrino emissions within the context of Pseudo-Scalar mediated Dark Matter interactions. Conversely, our work also includes a detailed comparison of several alternative models of Dark Matter interactions, including those involving Fermi, Vector, and Scalar mediators, as well as a novel scalar-meson-mediator interaction coupled to nucleon spin. The vast dataset collected by the CFIS project, comprising 234 sq.degrees of near-infrared data and ~1.1 billion galaxies at redshift 0.5-1.5, necessitates the development of efficient galaxy shape assessment tools to analyze its content. Introducing ShapePipe, a versatile pipeline designed to generate a range of useful galaxy characteristics that can be employed in various scientific studies, including weak-lensing computations and large-scale structure analyses. Shapes can be calculated using the IMMVALD algorithm, which is then validated through comparisons with other established methods like NGMFit and SHARP, as well as through cross-validation experiments. Furthermore, cross-correlations between E- and B-modes are established in the CFIS data, demonstrating the presence of a significant B-modes signal at ~10% of the E-modes signal power, all other factors held constant, with results in line with similar research in the same field. Finally, a cosmology analysis using ShapePipe-derived data and multiple lensing algorithms shows good agreement with the Planck 2018 cosmology, with results in line with similar research in the same field. Ultimately, the presence of a B-modes signal in the CFIS data and its subsequent cosmology analysis demonstrate that UNIONS/CFIS is suited for contributing to ongoing research in the ongoing CMB-Lensing Prize Challenge, among other applications. The ShapePipe pipeline is now publicly available at https://github.com/JulianElgGarcia/ShapePipe. A copy of the pipeline has also been installed on the C2P5 infrastructure at https://c2p5.gitub.io/ and is undergoing validation. We prove that a local complete intersection variety meeting certain conditions is k-rational and k-Du Bois, which stems from an analogous result for k-rational and k-Du Bois hypersurfaces. Specifically, k-rationality can be equated with the k-anness of the local cohomology rings for all relevant degrees, while k-Du Boisness can be equated with the k-anness of the local cohomology rings along with vanishing of certain higher degree cohomologies. Additionally, this study relates k-rationality to an extension of the k-anness property proposed by Ghezzi and Sheshadri for k < 2. Finally, this research offers examples illustrating non-trivial local complete intersection varieties that satisfy k-rationality or k-Du Boisness conditions, including an instance of k-rational but non-k-Du Bois variety for k = 3. Specifically, the instance is a quantic cuspidal rational double point with this k = 3. Conversely, this research also yields an example illustrating a k-Du Bois but non-k-rational variety, given by a quantic linear cone over an elliptic curve for k = 3. Building upon these findings and results, this study also explores some related broader inquiries, including a generalization of the k-rationality concept to singular varieties, along with examination of certain properties of k-rational varieties, including the quasicompactness of the Hilbert scheme of k-rational varieties and the k-rationality of certain fiber product varieties. Lastly, this research also raises queries and proposes conjectures concerning the relationships and generalizations of the k-ranness property in relation to the k-Du Boisness condition. Specifically, one proposed conjecture states that a quasiprojective variety could potentially be k-Du Bois only if it satisfies k-rationality conditions. In contrast, another proposed conjecture suggests that k-rationality should implicitly encompass k-Du Boisness, given sufficient conditions are met. In particular, one hypothetical implication could be that k-rational hypersurfaces are inherently k-Du Bois. Furthermore, another conjectured implication could be that k-rational complete intersections meeting certain conditions are inherently k-Du Bois. In a different direction, another proposed conjecture presents the hypothesis that k-rationality could be an implicit consequence of k-Du Boisness, given certain vanishing cohomology conditions are met. We are introducing the LAMOST Explorers survey, a new project that utilizes the LAMOST 4-meter telescope to conduct a large-scale spectroscopic survey of approximately 800,000 stars in the Galactic bulge and a surrounding area. This project began in October 2019 and will operate for 18 months, ultimately allowing scientists to investigate various phenomena including stellar evolution, the Galactic bulge's structure, the movement of stars, and the occurrence of microlensing events. During the initial data collection period, four LAMOST $K$2 plates were observed, and we have started to analyze the data, focusing on objects with adequate signal quality. After removing duplicates and objects outside the target range, we were left with about 66,000 stars. We used the LAMOST open data access policy to allow scientists to share their findings, and we have invited them to submit their initial research findings. One researcher has submitted data on HB stars, while another has submitted data on M giants. We also used the observed data to calculate the movement and variability of a group of RR Lyrae stars, and we found that their range of proper motion distribution significantly differs from previous research findings. Another researcher has discovered and identified 37 new RR Lyrae variable stars, and we used the observed data to calculate their characteristics, including periods, amplitudes, and phases. We used the observed data to create a database of RR Lyrae stars, and this database is available for public download. We believe that the LAMOST Explorers survey is an open and collaborative project, and we are eager to hear from you if you would like to use or contribute to the data. We especially welcome researchers to work on the data to study HB stars, M giants, and other types of stars. We are also planning to conduct a photo-multiplier analysis, and we are interested in hearing from you if you would like to participate. Creating truly random digits is crucial in generating high-quality pseudorandom numbers, which has far-reaching applications in cryptography and security. These pseudorandom numbers can be used as a secure substitute for truly random numbers in various contexts. Current methods for generating high-quality pseudorandom numbers typically rely on hardware-based approaches that are both efficient and secure. However, as technology progresses, finding an effective method to enhance entropy in digital circuits becomes increasingly important. In this research, we demonstrate that by reducing the supply voltage below its nominal value, the inherent randomness in SRAMs can be harnessed using SRAM-based architectures. Our proposed approach, TuRaN, showcases two such designs - one with multi-bit SRAM access and another with single-bit SRAM access - both of which successfully captured and visualized the generated random bits. Furthermore, our designs have exhibited exceptional quality in random bit sequences, outperforming existing standards in random number generation. Notably, the multi-bit SRAM access design has demonstrated an impressive entropy rate of 10.95 bits per bit, while the single-bit SRAM access design achieved an entropy rate of 10.86 bits per bit. Additionally, our work highlights the significant benefits of undervolting in promoting SRAM randomness, noting that the best results were obtained at approximately 70% of the nominal voltage. Ultimately, our research validates that undervolting can be leveraged to enhance entropy in digital circuits through SRAM-based microarchitectures. Additionally, the generated random bit sequences, as well as design files and compilation instructions, are publicly available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Furthermore, our work has been verified using three distinct tools - SIT, CEM, and TIS - to ensure the high quality of our single-bit SRAM access design. These verification tools confirmed our expectations, noting that the single-bit SRAM access design can withstand tests for centuries to come. In contrast, the multi-bit SRAM access design required only a few years to reach its maximum test duration. Nonetheless, our work has successfully extended the current benchmark in single-bit SRAM randomness to a multi-bit SRAM accessibility realm. In conclusion, our proposed TuRaN architecture has showcased its unparalleled performance in random bit generation, outperforming existing standards in supply voltage-based approaches. As such, TuRaN emerges as a cutting-edge solution for efficient and secure pseudorandom number generation. We have created a model for single-electron resistive switches using molecular structures and simulated their functionality to determine the reliability of two design variations, one involving a triple-junction geometry and another with a triple-dot island. By leveraging simulated results, we estimated that the triple-junction device could achieve an on-state to off-state transition success rate of around 80% and a substantial reduction in tripping voltage to as low as 0.5 volts due to the increased electrostatic coupling between junctions. Conversely, the triple-dot island design exhibited a higher failure rate compared to the triple-junction design, particularly due to the increased influence of quasi-particle pair creation on the middle island. Furthermore, we established that both designs can operate as nonvolatile single-electron transistors with a substantial signal amplification ratio. To validate our model's accuracy, we correlated it with experimental data from a particular molecular device, demonstrating a satisfactory match between simulated and actual results. Lastly, we explored the effects of varying operational parameters on the reliability of these devices and discovered that using a higher operating temperature could improve the failure rate but also increase the switching time. Conversely, utilizing a smaller dot or junction size can enhance the reliability and switch speed but makes the device more sensitive to operational temperature. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights for developing highly reliable and robust single-electron resistive switches at relatively low operating temperatures. However, further experimentation is needed to identify an adequate dot or junction size that balances reliability, switch speed, and operational temperature tolerance. Moreover, these simulations can be applied to a wide range of molecular structures beyond the specific compounds examined here. Leveraging extensive computational tools could provide valuable insights for designing novel molecular building blocks with exceptional single-electron resistive switching properties. Finally, our study demonstrates the relationship between the unusual behavior of space and the non-equilibrium statistical mechanics properties, which is a unique characteristic of artificial grids that mimic periodic structures in nature.

During the training process of a neural network, its architecture tends to develop a simpler structure, which is often attributed to the reduction of overfitting through regularization. We observed that neural networks utilizing complex architectures, such as complex activation functions or high dimensions, can achieve similar performance to simpler alternatives, reducing their complexity. We found this effect to be more pronounced in small datasets and observed a correlation with the complexity of the task at hand. We introduced a new concept, geometric intricacy, to quantify the level of complexity within a task, which can take various forms such as the properties of data or the structure of target outputs. We proposed several interpretations of geometric intricacy and demonstrated its relationship with the level of complexity imposed on neural networks. We further examined the relationship between regularization, geometric intricacy, and generalization performance, revealing a straightforward pattern: the level of complexity imposed on a neural network directly affects its generalization error. We validated our findings through extensive experiments across different scenarios, including the study of graph classification tasks. The discovery of geometric intricacy and its impact on generalization performance offers novel insights into the functioning of neural networks and their ability to generalize. It also presents a practical approach to control the level of complexity imposed on neural networks and thereby achieve better generalization performance in practice. This method is also adaptable for other $b\to c\mu^+\mu^-$ and $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ processes and can be extended with additional $B$ meson decays to increase its effectiveness. The marginal dependence framework is a versatile approach for modeling complex dependencies in a variable dimension framework. It consists of a group of models that can efficiently capture dependencies in high-dimensional data, particularly when dimensions exhibit non-parametric or parametric relationships. By assessing the marginalized effects of parameters on model behavior and structure, this framework offers beneficial properties such as parameter interpretability and statistical consistency. Within this framework, models that utilize Gaussian random fields provide a useful tool for practicing statisticians, offering a simple model structure and versatility in applications such as active learning and uncertainty quantification. However, the gain comes at the cost of decreased reliability and accuracy in predicting outcomes outside predicted spaces, a limitation that can be mitigated through Bayesian methods. This study aims to summarize the marginal dependence framework, focusing on linear models and Gaussian process regression, with a focus on theoretical advancements and practical applications. Furthermore, we will introduce novel innovations in this framework, specifically in the areas of variable selection, active learning, and uncertainty quantification, illustrating their efficiency through numerical studies and theoretical analysis. Finally, we will outline open problems and potential future areas of research within this framework. Through this work, we aim to provide accessible and comprehensive overview of the marginal dependence framework, empowering statisticians to efficiently learn dependent data structures in a variable dimension framework. This overview covers theoretical concepts, practical applications, and innovative model development, aiming to stimulate future research in this area. A prospective framework for intergenerational mobility considers the future opportunities of children when assessing parental influence, in contrast to the retrospective approach that focuses on past outcomes. To analyze prospects, a dynamic model of social mobility is developed, taking into account the uncertainty of future economic growth and the resulting variability in children's opportunities. A method is introduced to measure the effect of parental influence on the distribution of prospects through the comparison of children's opportunities in different parental groups, while accounting for the influence of parental resources. This approach is applied to an analysis of social mobility in the United States, using data from the Census and the Federal Reserve, and reveals a dynamic relationship between parental income and the distribution of children's opportunities. Unlike the findings of previous studies using retrospective approaches, no significant changes are found in the effect of parental income on the distribution of prospects in the period examined. However, this study's results differ from those of another dynamic analysis of social mobility, which also found no significant change in the effect of parental income but attributed this outcome to a decrease in the effect of parental resources over time. The symmetry principles of bosons and fermions dictate their behavior under permutations, which relates to the parity transformation in a specific way. According to non-relativistic quantum theory, the permutation symmetry of particles can be explained by referring to the parity transformation as a proxy. In this approach, bosons are equivalent to even-dimensional algebraic objects, whereas fermions correspond to fermions in a one-dimensional setting. By extending this logic to relativistic theory, one might expect the success of quantum field theory to be limited to descriptions of particles in odd spatial dimensions, due to the absence of a well-defined parity operation in even-dimensional spaces. However, a notable exception is QED in 2D, which can be reformulated using a 'parity proxy' similar to the 'discrete Lorentz proxy' recently introduced. As a result, bosonic fermions can be utilized in 2D QED to achieve gauge invariant descriptions, which may provide insights into fermion-boson duality, a phenomenon recently observed in 2D QED at low temperatures known as 'anyon superconductivity'. Given the potential for generalizing QED to 'parity proxy' bosons in 2D, which could lead to observations of bosonic fermions in everyday matter, a pressing question arises: can we detect parity, and thus bosonic fermions, in everyday matter? One possible way to do this is by utilizing observations of non-integer spin densities in condensed matter systems, which might be indicative of 'fermionic' bosons with half-integer spin. Ultimately, resolving this enigma may allow us to unlock 'anyon superconductivity' and the generalization of QED to 'parity proxy' bosions. Conversely, it is also possible that the break-through will come from the more conventional approach based on 'hidden' fermions. In this context, our work is a part of a broader research endeavor aimed at re-examining the foundational relationships between spin, statistics, and parity, which may yield unexpected insights into the underlying structure of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory. The equivalence constant $\varepsilon$ can be made arbitrarily small. This research extends a prior finding from Banach spaces to a specific case involving $\ell_p$ spaces, particularly when $X$ and $Y$ are isolated from the presence of null sequences. Additionally, we demonstrate that for $p=1$, this property no longer holds. Conversely, for $p>2$, we identify a particular inequality for which this dimension transformation maintains approximate isometry with an added constraint. These results build upon a related concept in linear algebra known as $\varepsilon$-isometry. Furthermore, we provide a related theorem concerning approximate isometry between subspaces of $\ell_p$ for $1<p<\infty$. To establish this, we adapt a related result concerning approximate isometry between subspaces of $C[0,1]$ from a prior publication by Bilyr and Li. Recent breakthroughs in neural network based modeling have led to remarkable advancements, surpassing previous expectations. However, there are certain tasks that dedicated expert models have been performing exceptionally well, particularly those trained on vast, publicly available datasets. Despite their prowess, expert models can benefit from incorporating additional information from specific, local data sets, which might not be accessible to them due to privacy concerns or data scarcity. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework that enables regular neural network models to leverage private data from expert models, using only publicly available data as input. By doing so, we enable these models to adapt to specific, local data sets, while still generalizing effectively. Notably, our approach can be applied across multiple knowledge sources and offers numerous versatile applications, as evidenced by our performance enhancements in sampling and inference. Furthermore, our methodology is comprehensive, providing detailed analysis and insights into its features. To demonstrate the adaptability of our approach, we utilized expert models from distinct fields, including computer vision and natural language processing. Our results show that our framework can seamlessly integrate the knowledge from these various domains, enhancing the overall outcome. A open-source implementation of our framework is available at https://github.com/dvdmueller/cdim. Future research will focus on exploring new applications and incorporating additional data-informed modeling strategies. To achieve this, we will establish a public repository of trained models from various specialized domains, dubbed the "Expert Model Repository". This resource will not only facilitate the reproduction of our work but also offer a vast collection of pre-trained models, enabling other researchers to build upon our approach in novel ways. Currently, the repository comprises over 300 models, each trained on over 10 million examples, and is continuously expanding with new additions. By providing this resource, we aim to establish a common language for expert models, promoting collaboration and innovation in the wider research community. A comprehensive guide to the repository is available at https://cdim-guide.dvdmueller.com. Future research will also concentrate on delving deeper into the underlying mechanics of expert models, particularly their generalization capabilities beyond their training data. To achieve this, we will examine multiple neural network models trained on different datasets varying in size, domain, and task, with a focus on understanding their common characteristics and how they evolve during training. A open-source implementation of our approach to analyze neural network models is available at https://github.com/dvdmueller/generalization. The source code for our website is hosted at https://github.com/dvdmueller/cdim-website

Advanced automotive electronics play a vital role in vehicle safety by preventing accidents, however, they can also give rise to critical hazards if compromised. To safeguard against malicious interference, automotive systems require robust security measures, particularly in the event of software failures. This research presents a novel technique known as prognostic safety filtering, which aims to ensure the reliability of software-coded functions in safety-critical systems. This method utilizes system-level synthesis and prognostics to create a resilient safety framework, thus preventing potential hazards from spreading to other system components. Initially, this approach is demonstrated on an aircraft engine health monitoring system and later applied to a mobile chassis control system, showcasing its efficacy through mathematical models and hardware-in-the-loop testing. This innovative safety protocol not only enhances safety but also enables resource optimization by pinpointing the minimum required resources for each scheduled task, thereby enabling dynamic memory allocation. Finally, this research highlights the practicality of this safety protocol by translating its concepts into a viable, verifiable design procedure. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that prognostic safety filtering can be achieved through a design of correct-by-construction safety protocols. This safety filter can be effectively modeled as a convex optimization problem, thereby enabling easy integration into existing design methodologies. This research sets the groundwork for incorporating safety filters into modern automotive electronic control units, thereby ensuring the safety of ongoing mission-critical operations. Safety validation tests are planned to validate the efficacy of this safety filter in real-world settings. Furthermore, this research lays the foundation for the development of safety filters tailored to specific application requirements, while also enabling the creation of customized safety validation test scenarios. Moving forward, this research will be expanded to encompass other safety-critical application areas, such as medical and industrial automation. Finally, this research is expected to contribute to the development of standardized safety protocols for the design and deployment of reliable software-coded systems. Ultimately, this research aims to promote the design of robust, safety-critical systems across various application domains. The effectiveness of a fully random phase source in the fully random phase source-based quantum key distribution system is explored under conditions of partial phase randomization. While partial randomization does not violate the system's security in principle, in practice it can be compromised if the full randomness is not achieved due to an attacker intercepting and controlling a portion of the phases. This could potentially allow the launch of a targeted attack, making the system vulnerable to breach. A specific scenario is examined where an attacker controls randomizations in 25% of the phases and it is found through numerical simulation that if less than 93% of the key data is used, a successful hack can be implemented, rendering the system insecure. However, if more than 93% of the key data is used, a successful hack becomes impossible, indicating a trade-off between remote connection distance and security in this system. This study confirms that fully random phase sources are not suitable for quantum key distribution and highlights the importance of using fully random phase sources instead. Moreover, this study provides a method for determining the critical point between remote connection distance and security, which is an invaluable tool for practical applications of quantum key distribution. Finally, this study suggests that while fully random phase sources do offer some level of security, they can also be compromised if particular conditions are not met, making them vulnerable to breach in specific scenarios. \end{document}

While large-scale language models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in out-of-context understanding, their performance in in-context learning has garnered significant attention due to its potential for limited-domain, task-specific applications. Nonetheless, research into the impact of training data on the in-context learning abilities of these models is underrepresented. To this end, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the effect of pretraining datasets on the in-context learning performance of a 13B-parameter language model, exploring the underpinning factors with substantial domain-specific implications. Moreover, we showcase the feasibility of in-context fine-tuning for limited-resource settings by achieving comparable performance to out-of-context training methods on CoQA, SQuAD, and WikiHops. Notably, our research highlights the significance of domain representation within the pretraining dataset for the in-context learning model to excel, attributing this phenomenon to the dynamic nature of task-specific concepts that require substantial domain examples for clear differentiation. Ultimately, our study sheds light on the intricate interplay between a model's training data and its in-context learning abilities. With these findings, we envision a prospective future where massive language models can be adaptively fine-tuned in-context to various tasks across different domains and cultures. Galaxy clusters across the sky exhibit diverse cooling patterns, ranging from active cooling in a few to no cooling at all in many. This distinction cannot be fully explained by existing theories, resulting in a significant discrepancy that needs to be resolved. To address this issue, a novel feedback mechanism involving the heating of intracluster media by the kinetic energy of turbulent motions has been proposed, leading to an improved understanding of the phenomenon. In this context, we introduce a highly advanced magnetohydrodynamic model that accounts for both radiative cooling and the impact of magnetic fields on condensation, as well as a previously unstudied process called thermal conduction. We then apply this model to three different types of galaxy groups, utilizing either numerical magnetohydrodynamic simulations or a specially designed fluid model to analyze their behavior. Our primary findings indicate that when magnetic fields are included, cooling is able to occur in greater densities than in their pure MHD counterparts, while the impact of thermal conduction tends to stabilize the ICM and prevents the condensation of cold clouds. We believe that the incorporation of kinetic turbulence in a more advanced simulation could further enhance our current understanding of the active cooling/no cooling discrepancy. Additionally, we propose that the active cooling/no cooling discrepancy, particularly in the active cooling regime, may be a transient state in a dynamic equilibrium between radiative cooling and thermal conduction. Based on our model's analysis, we predict that no active cooling will be observed within approximately 1.6 billion years. From an observational standpoint, we predict that no cool-core existence will be observed within approximately 2.2 billion years, a time frame that is roughly half as long as our initial estimate. The increasing complexity of 5G networks along with the growing number of 5G devices necessitates more automated and intelligent management systems to ensure seamless 5G service delivery. Our research focuses on developing efficient and sustainable 5G core networks through intelligent management strategies, including automated decision-making processes for 5G core network management. We propose self-administered strategies for key 5G core network management functions such as resource allocation, service quality management, and network slice management. The proposed management strategies are designed to be automatically adjustable in real-time according to changing service demands and environmental conditions like temperature and energy consumption. The optimization goals of these strategies include maximum resource utilization, optimal quality-of-service and service quality, high system performance, and minimal energy consumption to ensure a green and sustainable 5G network infrastructure. We evaluated the proposed strategies through simulations, and the results show significant improvements in resource utilization, quality-of-service and service quality, system performance, and energy consumption. Specifically, our best-performing resource allocation strategy achieved an average resource utilization rate of 93.6% for user equipment and 99.6% for network edge devices, a average quality-of-service of 4.87 ms and a average quality-of-service for services with high bandwidth consumption of 6.12 ms, a average system performance of 76.35% for network slice administration and an average power efficiency of 76.67% for energy consumption optimization. Furthermore, our core network management approaches can be generalized and applied to other problems in 5G core network management. The prevailing voice synthesis methods rely heavily on large datasets of annotated audio and text, mainly created by English speakers. Since acoustic units are the fundamental units of speech, examining the relationship between these units and the Exemplar Inventory in the PARC database reveals patterns consistent with speaker-independent annotation practices. Building on this insight, we have developed a method to create units from the audio features of speech without labels, which is feasible since the desired units are naturally discrete objects with distinct audio representations. This method entails growing clusters from seeds and is facilitated by the pre-existing annotation. Notably, we have successfully created voice synthesis datasets without labels for two languages, Arabic and Hindi, utilizing this approach, which are two languages for which labeled datasets are scarce and elusive. The resulting unsupervised datasets demonstrate comparable quality to supervised datasets in terms of prosodic features and mean opinion scores. Moreover, the semantic space of the synthesized speech is shown to resemble that of genuine speech, as examined using a variety of metrics, including calibration metrics and multilingual translation tables. This breakthrough has significant practical implications since it enables the creation of high-quality voice synthesis systems without extensive annotated data, making it more feasible to develop voice synthesis systems for languages with limited resources. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ameining/Unsupervised_VS.

In decentralized learning, a network of multiple nodes collaborates to minimize a shared objective function via message passing and information sharing. Unlike traditional centralized approaches, decentralized methods excel in large-scale learning environments where communication constraints apply. Nonetheless, they often struggle with changes in the available data, which can arise when new nodes join or existing nodes leave the network and receive replacement data. To adapt to such data shifts, a new communication-efficient method called DR-DSGD is proposed. DR-DSGD is an enhancement of the DSGD algorithm, allowing it to be robust against variations in the data distribution across the network. By employing a new averaging technique for aggregating information, DR-DSGD successfully minimizes the impact of changes in the data distribution, thus protecting the model from adverse effects of data shifts. Notably, DR-DSGD demands no further computational resources than DSGD and operates without the need for global information. Moreover, it is compatible with a wide range of distributed stochastic gradient descent algorithms. To validate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD, it is tested on different graph topologies and various data distribution changes, including Dirichlet and K-Dirichlet distributions. The results show that DR-DSGD significantly outperforms DSGD and other baseline decentralized learning methods in resisting data shifts, while maintaining comparable performance in stable environments. The source code of DR-DSGD is available at https://github.com/ArashLalezari/DR-DSGD for the convenience of the research community. Experimental findings, including codes and datasets used in this research, can also be accessed via https://github.com/ArashLalezari/DR-DSGD. Additional information is available at my personal website: https://alalezarash.github.io/. Key contributions of this research have been summarized as follows. Firstly, a new challenge in decentralized learning has been identified and defined, specifically the distributional change robustness of decentralized algorithms. Secondly, DR-DSGD has been proposed as a decentralized learning algorithm capable of effectively resisting data shifts while requiring minimal computational resources. Thirdly, the effectiveness of DR-DSGD has been validated through comprehensive experimental studies. Lastly, the source code of DR-DSGD has been made available to facilitate future research. To further explore this research, several possible directions have been suggested. Firstly, developing new communication protocols to enhance the performance of decentralized learning algorithms. Secondly, investigating distribution changes in the context of other machine learning tasks, such as classification. Thirdly, extending the concept of distributional change robustness

In computer vision, a comprehensive object description encompasses not just where an object is located, but also its shape and what it constitutes. We draw inspiration from the fundamental principles of geometry and classification to develop an analytical framework for a complete 3D object understanding. We propose an innovative method, Category-level Object Pose and Form Estimator (COPF), capable of accurately determining an object's position, structure, and category from both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints, even in the absence of complete 3D information. By leveraging a reliable geometric model, we demonstrate that an object's shape can be inferred solely from its keypoints, and we introduce a novel metric for evaluating 3D object detection models. We also create the Resilient Category-level Perception challenge to promote the development of robust and adaptable multi-task models, encompassing both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints. Through extensive testing on various datasets, including the Resilient Generation of Category-level Object Pose and Form challenge datasets and the SUN3D dataset, we show that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines and achieves robust results across a range of scenarios. We introduce a novel, general framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point clouds. PRNet is based on a self-supervised learning approach that derives a suitable loss function from raw data, eliminating the need for time-consuming annotations. The framework consists of two main components - a geometric module and a cross-correlation module - that work together to derive reliable correspondences. The geometric module applies normalized convolution to capture local shape characteristics, while the cross-correlation module uses flexible queries to identify suitable matches. Notably, PRNet learns correspondences that are invariant to rotation, thus producing more accurate results under different viewpoints. Our method demonstrates superior performance on various benchmarks and generates robust correspondences even in complex scenarios. The code will be publicly available soon.

Recent research has focused on generating future actions in video clips to create more realistic and forward-looking generative models. Unlike existing methods that only utilize consecutive frames for prediction, our approach leverages a radial basis function (RBF) kernelized feature mapping technique to incorporate both spatial and temporal information from videos. We tested our approach on datasets consisting of NTU-RGB+Motion and Dynamec and found that it outperformed state-of-the-art models on nearly all tasks. Notably, our method achieved perfect accuracy in predicting the next joint angle in the Dynamec dataset, demonstrating its ability to generate precise and detailed movement sequences. While our approach demonstrated remarkable results, it did not consistently surpass existing methods on all tasks, highlighting its versatility and applicability to a range of challenging video-based prediction tasks. Neural network-based point cloud models have shown significant performance gains, with a particular advantage in tasks like object classification and object detection. However, these models are prone to misclassifying noisy data, with smoothing methods proving to be an effective solution. Previous smoothing techniques have focused on removing outliers by incorporating neighboring data, but they disregard the geometric structure of the point cloud in their models. In contrast, this study proposes TPC, a novel outlierness classifier that utilizes a multi-layer perceptron to identify noisy data based on geometric transformations such as translation, rotation, and scaling. By incorporating this outlierness classifier into a context encoder for point clouds, TPC can be trained, and it is applied in a post-processing stage to filter outliers from the point cloud representation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TPC in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, with significant improvement in classification accuracy from 82.72% to 84.28% on S3DIS. Additionally, TPC shows applicability in object detection, with a Method 2 version achieving top-1 accuracy of 88.7% on nuScenes, outperforming a benchmark model without outlierness filtering. A code repository for TPC is available at https://github.com/heyang2009/TPC.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a prominent research area in
representing knowledge graphs with evolving entities and temporal properties.
Building upon the success of knowledge graph completion in static settings, we
investigate the extension to temporal knowledge graphs by adopting a simple and
general framework for modeling time-dependent relationships. We achieve this
goal by utilizing low-rank and model-independent representations of temporal
knowledge graphs, which can be applied to various ranking methods. Notably, we
show that existing approaches relying on complete snapshots of knowledge graphs
suffer from degraded performance when dealing with temporal aspects, but by
treating temporal information as a low-rank update, we enhance existing models.
Using the NGBP dataset, we demonstrate that our proposed solution excels in
temporal knowledge graph completion when compared to existing knowledge graph
completion methods. Furthermore, we provide evidence that our approach can
be successfully applied to other ranking tasks in knowledge graphs, thus
emphasizing its model-independent value. The code for NGBP is available at

Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in removing ground noise and enhancing audio quality. We investigate the generalized k-center problem under various metrics. Our study distinguishes between doubling and highway measures, impacting the scalability of approximation algorithms in metric spaces. A doubling measure indicates the maximum factor by which a region can be split into smaller areas, whereas a highway measure represents a major pathway in an isometry group of a metric space. Approximately 20 years ago, Feige and Farach-Colton presented an approximation algorithm for the k-center problem with a O(log k) factor in doubling spaces. Our research contradicts a hypothesis suggesting this approximation algorithm is the best possible by demonstrating an even simpler O(log^2 k) approximation algorithm in doubling spaces. Our analysis relies on three key concepts: a min-{1/ε}-spanner construction, approximate doubling dimension reduction, and a new measure of highway groups' size. We show the first two concepts lead to an even simpler O(log k) approximation algorithm in doubling spaces. Our min-{1/ε}-spanner construction, a concept previously used to improve approximation algorithms for set cover, might be independently valuable. We also present an even simpler O(log k) approximation algorithm in doubling spaces using a min-{1/ε}-spanner and reduced doubling space dimension. Our work implies that further improvements in doubling spaces likely won't occur without addressing the underlying geometric issues. We also explore the generalized k-center problem in highway measure spaces, presenting an even simpler O(log k) approximation algorithm based on doubling space results and illustrating its failure in certain highway measure spaces. Our study suggests approximating doubling measures by sampling measures with well-connected pathways may be necessary to improve highway measure results. We demonstrate an even simpler O(log k) approximation algorithm in highway measure spaces using a sampling approach. Our min-{1/ε}-spanner construction and approximate doubling dimension reduction concepts lead to even simpler approximations in highway measure spaces. Our work implies that doubling measure results are direct consequences of approximating spanners and may be useful in other applications. We also discuss potential connections between our approximations and the Plank problem. Our approximations might provide an alternative solution if we can approximate doubling measures efficiently. Our study explores the generalized k-center problem's approximability in doubling and highway measure spaces, illustrating the significant difference between these spaces in approximability. We present even simpler approximations for both spaces, revealing various limitations in approximability. Our approximations might be useful in understanding the computational complexity of generalized k-center problem. Our study provides even simpler approximations for both doubling and highway measure spaces.

We investigate the problem of accurately estimating a scale parameter in large networks, particularly those exhibiting the characteristics of small-world graphs, in the presence of malicious and untrusted nodes. This involves developing robust network scale estimation algorithms that can withstand malicious interference and enable secure communication among nodes within the network. Leveraging the concept of a scale parameter from random graph theory, we create a novel objective function that correlates network scale with the ratio of long-to-short path lengths in the graph. Building on this framework, we develop several robust estimation algorithms using techniques such as majority voting and distribution analysis. Notably, our results show that a low-degree estimator can achieve nearly optimal performance even in the presence of malicious nodes, while an alternative estimator may produce biased outcomes in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we examine the practical implementation of these algorithms in various graph models and demonstrate their resilience and accuracy under different attack scenarios. Experimentation-based evidence confirms the efficacy of our proposed algorithms for scale estimation in large networks, particularly in the ER graph model. Additionally, we explore the parameter dependence of our methods in the Watts-Strogatz graph model and highlight the importance of balancing algorithm parameters to produce reliable estimates. Moreover, we investigate the limiting behavior of our algorithms under controlled attack scenarios and verify their ability to produce accurate estimates even in the presence of malicious nodes. Lastly, we compare the performance of our proposed algorithms on real-world graph datasets and showcase their resilience and accuracy in various node attack scenarios. Overall, our study contributes novel scale estimation algorithms that achieve optimal performance in large networks, particularly those exhibiting the characteristics of small-world graphs, while remaining resilient to malicious and untrusted nodes. These algorithms may have practical applications in secure network communication and surveillance systems.
